q: Is it possible to transfer a running process to your terminal?
ref:
You can revoke “ownership” of the program from the shell with the disown built-in:

# press Ctrl+Z to suspend the program
bg
disown

However this only tells the shell not to send a SIGHUP signal to the program when the shell exits. The program will retain any connection it has with the terminal, usually as standard input, output and error streams. There is no way to reattach those to another terminal. (Screen works by emulating a terminal for each window, so the programs are attached to the screen window.)

It is possible to reattach the filedescriptors to a different file by attaching the program in a debugger (i.e. using ptrace) and making it call open, dup and close. There are a few tools that do this; this is a tricky process, and sometimes they will crash the process instead. The possibilities include (links collected from answers to How can I disown a running process and associate it to a new screen shell? and Can I nohup/screen an already-started process?):

grab (and the more ambitious cryopid)

neercs

reredirect

reptyr

retty
ans:
Not simply, no. You can’t pass a running process from one shell/terminal to another, and `disown` does not reattach it; it only stops the shell from sending SIGHUP when it exits.

You can suspend it with `Ctrl+Z`, resume it in the background with `bg`, and then `disown`, but it will still keep its original terminal I/O.

If you need it attached to another terminal or `screen` session after the fact, that generally isn’t possible normally. Some tools like `reptyr`, `grab`, `neercs`, `reredirect`, or `retty` may help, but they’re tricky and can crash the process.

q: What is the meaning of $* in a shell script?
ref:
Interpretation of *.* under old Windows/DOS systems

The significance here is more related to Windows/DOS than to Unix/Linux. On old Windows/DOS systems it was a 'wildcard' pattern. Wildcard patterns were used for matching filenames in a similar manner to Unix globs. The *.* wildcard was commonly used to match any file.

As with a Unix glob, the * will match any sequence of characters in a filename, as such * on its own will also match any file. However the reason why *.* will match any filename too is due to differences in the way that these wildcards work. According to this article:

Any characters other than a dot that come after an asterisk have no effect, since the asterisk moves the cursor to position 12, at which point nothing changes the parse state except for a dot, which clears the last three positions and moves the cursor.

This behaviour (somewhat odd from Unix perspective) means that a dot following a * does not actually match a dot, but is just a hackish way to allow you to add more characters to the pattern. This means that adding another * will match anything in these last three positions.

This makes a little more sense when you consider that the syntax was used on DOS and old Windows systems before Windows 95 which required 8.3 filenames. These filenames were only allowed to have one dot and at most three characters following the dot. Most, if not all files on the system would have a three character extension (even though technically a shorter or no extensio
ans: The provided information does not explain $* in a shell script. It only covers *.* as an old DOS/Windows wildcard pattern and * as a Unix-style filename wildcard. If you meant shell parameter expansion, I can’t confirm its meaning from this information alone.

q: Can a superuser (with 'root' access) manipulate data on a database installed on the server?
ref:
Negative ACLs

You can prevent a user from accessing certain parts of the filesystem by setting access control lists. For example, to ensure that the user abcd cannot access any file under /home:

setfacl -m user:abcd:0 /home

This approach is simple, but you must remember to block access to everything that you don't want abcd to be able to access.

Chroot

To get positive control over what abcd can see, set up a chroot, i.e. restrict the user to a subtree of the filesystem.

You need to make all the files that the user needs (e.g. mysql and all its dependencies, if you want the user to be able to run mysql) under the chroot. Say the path to the chroot is /home/restricted/abcd; the mysql program needs to be available under /home/restricted/abcd. A symbolic link pointing outside the chroot is no good because symbolic link lookup is affected by the chroot jail. Under Linux, you can make good use of bind mounts:

mount --rbind /bin /home/restricted/abcd/bin
mount --rbind /dev /home/restricted/abcd/dev
mount --rbind /etc /home/restricted/abcd/dev
mount --rbind /lib /home/restricted/abcd/lib
mount --rbind /proc /home/restricted/abcd/proc
mount --rbind /sbin /home/restricted/abcd/sbin
mount --rbind /sys /home/restricted/abcd/sys
mount --rbind /usr /home/restricted/abcd/usr

You can also copy files (but then you'll need to take care that they're up to date).

To restrict the user to the chroot, add a ChrootDirectory directive to /etc/sshd_config.

Match User abcd
    ChrootDirectory
ans:
Yes. A superuser with root access can manipulate data on a database installed on the server, because root is not restricted by the kind of directory-level access controls described here.

The supported guidance here is about limiting a regular user’s filesystem access with ACLs or a chroot jail. If the user needs to run programs like mysql, the evidence says chroot is the better fit, but it does not describe a way to stop root from accessing the database.

q: sudo nt passing after redirection operator
ref:
It is normal. The file after the > is not open by the process running under sudo, but by the shell, which isn't. Try this instead:

printf "foo" | sudo tee /etc/file
ans:
`sudo` applies to the command, not to the shell redirection. The shell opens `>` before `sudo` runs, so the file is accessed as your normal user and can fail with “Permission denied.”

For example, `sudo echo "xyz" >/etc/file` elevates only `echo`, not the redirection. Use a root process to do the write, such as:

`printf "xyz" | sudo tee /etc/file`

Or use a command/editor that opens the target file itself with elevated privileges.

q: problem occur during installation of moses scripts
ref:
This kind of message is usually due to a buggy shebang line, either an extra carriage return at the end of the first line or a BOM at the beginning of it.

Run:

$ head -1 yourscript | od -c

and see how it ends.

This is wrong:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n

This is wrong too:

0000000 357 273 277   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

This is correct:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

Use dos2unix (or sed, tr, awk, perl, python…) to fix your script if this is the issue.

Here is one that will remove both of a BOM and tailing CRs:

sed -i '1s/^.*#//;s/\r$//' brokenScript

Note that the shell you are using to run the script will slightly affect the error messages that are displayed.
Here are three scripts just showing their name (echo $0) and having the following respective shebang lines:

correctScript:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

scriptWithBom:

0000000 357 273 277   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

scriptWithCRLF:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n

Under bash, running them will show these messages:

$ ./correctScript
./correctScript
$ ./scriptWithCRLF
bash: ./scriptWithCRLF: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
$ ./scriptWithBom
./scriptWithBom: line 1: #!/bin/bash: No such file or directory
./scriptWithBom

Running the buggy ones by explicitely calling the interpreter allows the CRLF script to run without any issue:

$
ans:
This usually means the script’s shebang is broken, not that /bin/bash is actually missing. Check whether the first line has Windows CR line endings or a UTF-8 BOM.

You can inspect it with:

head -1 yourscript | od -c

If you see \r before \n, convert it to Unix line endings, for example with dos2unix. If there’s a BOM, remove that too.

A workaround is to run it with:

bash script.sh

That bypasses the shebang.

q: no such file or directory
ref: cd ~ /generallstuff should be cd ~/generallstuff, otherwise you will change into your home directory instead.
ans:
If you’re seeing “no such file or directory” even though the file exists, the issue may be in the path you’re using. For example, `cd ~ /generallstuff` is wrong because the space makes it act like `cd ~` plus a separate `/generallstuff`, so you stay in your home directory instead of the target folder.

Use:

q: Disk space shows up as used but not on `du`
ref:
Several possibilities.

a) scp may not have copied hidden files/directories; hard to tell w/o
knowing your data, seeing how you invoked scp.

b) another scenario will be that the filesystems use different block-sizes, and du doesn't add up the files byte sizes, it measures occupied disk space.
ans:
`du` reports occupied disk space, which can differ from simple file size totals. So space can show as used even when the `du` number seems smaller or doesn’t match what you expect, especially if filesystem block sizes differ between machines. Also, if files were copied with a method like `scp -r`, hidden files or directories may have been missed, making the directory appear smaller than the actual used space.

If you’re trying to verify what was copied, compare the actual file contents and sizes rather than relying only on `du`.

q: upgrade OpenSSL from 0.9.8w to 1.0.0i or 1.0.1a on Linux server
ref:
It is not possible without updating most of the system.  I tried the same with a CentOS 5.x and ended up wasting a lot of time.

What you could do (tried this, too, but ended up upgrading the whole system instead) is to install the sources of OpenSSL and your web server etc. -- whatever you wish to run with your new SSL, then compile these with a different compile root, e.g. in /opt. ans:
The safest guidance is not to try to upgrade OpenSSL in place on an old Linux system. The supported approach is to upgrade the whole system, since updating OpenSSL alone often forces you to update many dependent components too.

If you need a workaround, the closest supported options are:
- build OpenSSL and the services that need it in a separate prefix such as /opt
- compile those services against a static OpenSSL build
- run the service in a VM with a newer OS

There isn’t an easy, recommended RPM-only or script-based upgrade path for this case.

q: Create alias that can interact with arguments
ref:
Aliases are like commands in that all arguments to them are passed as arguments to the program they alias. For instance:

alias ls='ls -l -a -t -r'
# This now executes 'ls -l -a -t -r foo bar'
ls foo bar

If you want to have actual control over how the arguments are interpreted, then you could write a function like so:

my_program_wrapper() {
    local first_arg=$1 \
          second_arg=$2

    shift 2 # get rid of the first two arguments

    # ...

    /path/to/my_program "$@"
}
ans:
Yes, but only in a limited way. An alias doesn’t accept parameters like a function does; any arguments you type after the alias are passed through to the underlying command.

If you need to use, reorder, or otherwise control arguments, use a shell function instead. For example:

my_program_wrapper() {
    local first_arg=$1
    local second_arg=$2
    shift 2
    /path/to/my_program "$@"
}

So the practical answer is: aliases can forward arguments, but functions are the right choice for interacting with them.

In your second example, by placing var and var2 on separate lines, this makes the command the same as

  `while' COMMANDS has an exit status of zero.
  Exit Status: Returns the status of the last command executed.  

On the other hand, when a variable assignment precedes a command (in this case read), and that assignment is only followed by whitespace, the scope of that variable is local to the command ONLY! (internally)...

See:  In 'while IFS= read..', why does IFS have no effect?
ans:
If the loop is part of a pipeline, the commands in that loop may run in a separate subshell, so any variable changes inside the loop won’t affect the parent shell. That’s consistent with the earlier case: variables assigned in the shell itself persist, but temporary command-style assignments don’t.

Closest guidance: avoid piping into a `while` loop if you need local variable changes to remain after the loop. Instead, use redirection or another structure that keeps the loop in the current shell.

q: Use a shell variable to execute a comand
ref:
Either use export to turn it into an environment variable, or pass it directly to the command.

VAR="Test" sh -c 'echo "Hello $VAR"'

VAR="Test"
export VAR
sh -c 'echo "Hello $VAR"'

Avoid using double quotes around the shell code to allow interpolation as that introduces command injection vulnerabilities like in:

sh -c " echo 'Hello $VAR' "

causing a reboot if called when $VAR contains something like ';reboot #
ans:
Set the variable as an environment variable before starting the child shell, or export it first.

Example:
VAR="Test" sh -c 'echo "Hello $VAR"'

Or:
VAR="Test"
export VAR
sh -c 'echo "Hello $VAR"'

Use single quotes around the shell code so your current shell doesn’t expand it. Avoid double-quoted shell code, since that can allow command injection if the variable contains special characters.

q: Copy file over existing SSH session?
ref:
Master connection

It's easiest if you plan in advance.

Open a master connection the first time. For subsequent connections, route slave connections through the existing master connection. In your ~/.ssh/config, set up connection sharing to happen automatically:

ControlMaster auto
ControlPath ~/.ssh/control:%h:%p:%r

If you start an ssh session to the same (user, port, machine) as an existing connection, the second session will be tunneled over the first. Establishing the second connection requires no new authentication and is very fast.

So while you have your active connection, you can quickly:

copy a file with scp or rsync;

mount a remote filesystem with sshfs.

Forwarding

On an existing connection, you can establish a reverse ssh tunnel. On the ssh command line, create a remote forwarding by passing -R 22042:localhost:22 where 22042 is a randomly chosen number that's different from any other port number on the remote machine. Then ssh -p 22042 localhost on the remote machine connects you back to the source machine; you can use scp -P 22042 foo localhost: to copy files.

You can automate this further with RemoteForward 22042 localhost:22. The problem with this is that if you connect to the same computer with multiple instances of ssh, or if someone else is using the port, you don't get the forwarding.

If you haven't enabled a remote forwarding from the start, you can do it on an existing ssh session. Type Enter ~C Enter -R 22042:localhost:22 Enter.
See “Escape charac
ans:
Yes, if you planned for it or can set it up on the existing SSH session.

Two supported options are:
- Use SSH connection sharing, so a second ssh/scp/rsync connection to the same host reuses the active one.
- Set up a reverse tunnel on the current session with `-R`, or add it live with `~C`, then copy back through `localhost` on the remote machine.

For example, with a reverse tunnel you can run `scp -P 22042 foo localhost:` from the remote machine to send the file to your local system.

q: man pages: meaning of '2' in STAT(2)?
ref:
The number corresponds to what section of the manual that page is from; 1 is user commands, while 8 is sysadmin stuff. The man page for man itself (man man) explains it and lists the standard ones:

MANUAL SECTIONS
    The standard sections of the manual include:

    1      User Commands
    2      System Calls
    3      C Library Functions
    4      Devices and Special Files
    5      File Formats and Conventions
    6      Games et. al.
    7      Miscellanea
    8      System Administration tools and Daemons

    Distributions customize the manual section to their specifics,
    which often include additional sections.

There are certain terms that have different pages in different sections (e.g. printf as a command appears in section 1, as a stdlib function appears in section 3); in cases like that you can pass the section number to man before the page name to choose which one you want, or use man -a to show every matching page in a row:

$ man 1 printf
$ man 3 printf
$ man -a printf

You can tell what sections a term falls in with man -k (equivalent to the apropos command). It will do substring matches too (e.g. it will show sprintf if you run man -k printf), so you need to use ^term to limit it:

$ man -k '^printf'
printf               (1)  - format and print data
printf               (1p)  - write formatted output
printf               (3)  - formatted output conversion
printf               (3p)  - print formatted output
printf [builtins]    (1)  - bash built-in com
ans: The “2” is the man-page section number. Section 2 covers system calls. So STAT(2) means the stat-related page in section 2. If a name exists in multiple sections, you can specify the section, like `man 2 stat` or `man 3 printf`.

q: Different representation of bash in 'ps -f' command
ref:
The problem is that cut uses a single space character as a delimiter, but as the column name and the 4 digit PIDs are right aligned there are multiple leading spaces which cause cut to output an empty line.

An alternative approach is to use awk, which copes better with this kind of input:

ps | awk '{ print $1 }'

In the case of ps in particular mindthemonkey's answer is a better approach.
ans:
In `ps -f`, these usually refer to the same shell program, but with different display forms.

`bash` means the process name is shown as just `bash`.

`-bash` usually means a login shell; the leading `-` is commonly used to indicate that.

`/bin/bash` shows the full path to the executable instead of just the command name.

The exact `ps` display can vary by context, so the formatting may not be consistent across systems or commands.

q: How can I rename all files in the current directory having a particular extension to another extension?
ans:
Use `find` with `-execdir` and a `rename` pattern that handles the `./` prefix it passes:

```sh
find . -depth -execdir rename 's/^(\.\/[^.]*)\.(.*)$/\U$1\E.$2/' {} \;
```

If you only want files in the current directory, use `find .` as shown. This renames files by changing the extension in the matched names, and the `-depth`/`-execdir` combination makes it work recursively if needed.

q: deal with file names with "-" as beginning on linux
ref:
Using - as a filename to mean stdin/stdout is a convention that a lot of programs use. It is not a special property of the filename. The kernel does not recognise - as special so any system calls referring to - as a filename will use - literally as the filename.

With bash redirection, - is not recognised as a special filename¹, so bash will use that as the literal filename.

When cat sees the string - as a filename, it treats it as a synonym for stdin. To get around this, you need to alter the string that cat sees in such a way that it still refers to a file called -. The usual way of doing this is to prefix the filename with a path - ./-, or /home/Tim/-. This technique is also used to get around similar issues where command line options clash with filenames, so a file referred to as ./-e does not appear as the -e command line option to a program, for example.

¹ Except for the >& filename operator that bash eventually copied from csh to redirect both stdout and stderr, where >&- is still about closing file descriptors like in the Bourne shell, even when - is quoted or the result of an expansion which means that >& operator can't be used for arbitrary file names. Use the standard/Bourne > "$file" 2>&1 syntax or the bash-specific &> "$file" instead.
ans:
If a filename starts with `-`, commands may read it as an option. Use a path prefix like `./` or tell the command that options are over with `--`.

Examples:
- `mv -- ./- newname`
- `cat ./-`

This applies similarly to names beginning with `--`: prefix with `./` so the program treats it as a filename, not an option.

q: sudo here-document / concatenation?
ref:
If you want to write a here-doc and you don't want ANY of the doc to be expanded or any special characters interpreted, you can quote the label with single quotes, like this:

$ cat >file <<'EOF'
echo "$ABC=home_dir"
EOF

However, your situation as described in your example is much more complex, because you're really sending this content through ssh, to a remote system, to be run by sudo which is also invoking a shell (and so that shell will expand the content as well).  You're going to need more levels of quoting to get this right, but even with that it still won't work because sudo requires a terminal (so it can ask for a password) and you've redirected from stdin.  Even using ssh -t won't help here.

Also I agree with Johan.  It's not clear this is really what you want; note that it's not legal to assign a value to a shell variable reference, so if this file you're trying to create is supposed to be a shell script, it won't work as you've described it.  Maybe if you back up a bit and describe what you really want to do, we can help more.
ans:
A quoted here-doc like `<<'EOF'` stops local expansion, so `$ABC` is kept literally.

For `ssh ... sudo ...` or similar nested commands, each shell still has its own parsing and expansion, so you need to quote for every layer that will interpret the text. A simple here-doc alone won’t prevent remote expansion after `ssh`.

Also, `sudo` may fail with stdin redirection because it often wants a terminal for password entry, so here-doc input can break that.

If you want a literal `$`, quote the here-doc delimiter. If you want a remote command to see text unchanged, you must preserve quoting through all intermediate shells.

q: Disk space shows up as used but not on `du`
ref:
du == Disk Usage. It walks through directory tree and counts the sum size of all files therein. It may not output exact information due to the possibility of unreadable files, hardlinks in directory tree, etc. It will show information about the specific directory requested. Think, "How much disk space is being used by these files?"

df == Disk Free. Looks at disk used blocks directly in filesystem metadata. Because of this it returns much faster that du but can only show info about the entire disk/partition. Think, "How much free disk space do I have?"
ans:
`du` and `df` measure different things.

`du` totals the files it can see under the directory tree you point it at. `df` reports used blocks for the whole filesystem or partition.

So if `df` shows about 20G more used space than `du`, that extra space is likely usage not included in that directory view, because `df` reflects the filesystem’s actual block usage for the partition.

q: How to recover a backgrounded job from a previous shell?
ref: Spawn your script within a screen session. Redirect output to TTY as you proposed. Detach from the screen session and close the terminal. No SIGHUP will be sent so the script should continue to run.
ans:
Not directly. The supported guidance here is to use `screen` to keep the command attached to a terminal-like session from the start, run it there, and detach when needed. That avoids SIGHUP when the terminal closes.

If the job has already been disowned or the shell is gone, this does not provide a way to re-attach it to the tty. The closest supported option is to start interactive jobs inside `screen` beforehand rather than trying to recover them afterward.

q: File extensions and association with programs in linux
ref:
This can be done easily in the shell, starting in the subdir and moving upwards:

f=/root/subfolder1/subfolder2/subfolderN
while [[ $f != / ]]; do chmod +rx "$f"; f=$(dirname "$f"); done;

This starts with whatever file/directory you set f too, and works on every parent directory, until it encounters "/" (or whatever you set the string in the condition of the loop to). It does not chmod "/". Make sure both f and the directory in the condition of the loop are absolute paths.
ans:
In Linux, file extensions are not what determines how a program is associated with a file; associations are usually based on file type, permissions, or desktop MIME settings.

The closest supported guidance here is to use a shell loop to traverse paths and act on each matching item, rather than handling files one by one manually. For example, the earlier pattern shows walking up directories with a `while` loop and applying a command at each step.

If you want, I can help adapt that general loop pattern to files matching a specific extension in subfolders.

q: Is it possible to download a file locally when I've already ssh'ed into a remote computer?
ref:
I take it host B is e.g. a gateway in an intranet and can connect to host A and C, e.g. like this:

                                                                       -----------------------------------------------------------
                                                                      |                                                           |
                                                                      |                                                           |
                       ---------                                -----------                    --------------                     |
                      |A        |------------------------------|   B       |------------------|              |                    |
                       ---------                               |           |                  | C            |                    |
                                                                -----------                    --------------                     |
                                                                      |                                                           |
                                                                       -----------------------------------------------------------

In this case the best solution is ssh port forwarding. I describe it at http://www.linuxintro.org/wiki/Tunneling_with_OpenSSH

First, on A, you tunnel B's port 2222 to C's port 22 with the command:

ssh -L 2222:C:
ans: Yes, but not directly from the interactive SSH shell. The supported way is to use SSH port forwarding so the remote SSH service is tunneled through the host, then connect to the forwarded port and transfer the file through that tunnel. This is fine for simple, occasional copying. If that isn’t practical, the only other method mentioned is manually piping data with `cat > target_file`.

q: Undo safely remove device
ref:
If you delete /usr/lib, you will kill your system as very crucial libraries reside in this directory. Like the LibC library which is used by all binaries. So it is unlikely that you will be able to something.
(If you are lucky and interrupted the command with a quick CTRL+C before is comletion, maybe only sub-dirs are deleted and the LibC is still there)

If the system is totally blocked (login impossible, boot fails, ...), let's hope that you have a Live CD of the same distribution and the same version under the hand.

Boot from this CD, mount the filesystem of your hard-disk and copy the /usr/lib from the Live system to the one on the hard-disk.
ans:
There usually isn’t a direct undo for a removal action that deleted files. If you acted quickly, some files or subdirectories may still remain, and the system may still work.

If the system is broken, boot from a Live CD of the same distribution and version, mount the hard-disk filesystem, and copy back the missing files or /usr/lib from the Live system.

If the system still boots, the closest recovery option is to restore the deleted files from a backup or another copied source.

q: How does the syntax "${foo##*.}" work to get file extensions?
ref:
That is called parameter expansion:

$3 is your variable, which is the third parameter of the script/function.

# will remove the shortest prefix of the variable.

? is the pattern you are looking for (in this case is any character).

So basically you remove the shortest prefix of the variable named 3 until you find the pattern.

In general, we can consider:

${variable_name[option][pattern]}

There are other options like:

## remove largest prefix.

% remove shortest suffix.

%% remove largest suffix.

Which you can combine with other patterns, for example, for getting the last field of a CSV line:

> string="asdf,1234,aa,foo22"
> echo ${string##*,}
foo22

Notice how we have removed the largest prefix searching for the pattern "any character(s) followed by a comma".
ans:
`${foo##*.}` is Bash parameter expansion.

It removes the longest matching prefix ending with a literal dot from `foo`. In practice, `*` matches any characters up to the last `.` and the part after that dot is returned, which is the file extension.

Example: if `foo=file.tar.gz`, then `${foo##*.}` gives `gz`.

If `foo` contains no dot, it returns the original value unchanged.

q: Permanent Environment Variable for all users
ref:
You have to put the declaration in the initialization files of your shell:

If you are using bash, ash, ksh or some other Bourne-style shell, you can add

ABC="123"; export ABC

in your .profile file (${HOME}/.profile). This is the default situation on most Unix installations, and in particular on Debian. 

If your login shell is bash, you can use .bash_profile (${HOME}/.bash_profile) or .bash_login instead. 

Note: If either of these files exists and your login shell is bash, .profile is not read when you log in over ssh or on a text console, but it might still be read instead of .bash_profile if you log in from the GUI. Also, if there is no .bash_profile, then use .bashrc.

If you've set zsh as your login shell, use ~/.zprofile instead of ~/.profile.

If you are using tcsh, add

setenv ABC "123"

in .login file (${HOME}/.login)

if you are using another shell look at the shell manual how to define environment variables and which files are executed at the shell startup.
ans:
The resolved guidance only covers setting environment variables permanently for one user by adding them to that user’s shell startup file, such as `~/.profile` for bash/Bourne-style shells, `~/.bash_profile` or `~/.bash_login`, `~/.bashrc` in some cases, `~/.zprofile` for zsh, or `~/.login` for tcsh.

It does not say how to set a variable permanently for all users. The closest supported guidance is that you would need a system-wide method instead of a per-user startup file, but that method is not specified here.

q: Undo safely remove device
ref:
If you delete /usr/lib, you will kill your system as very crucial libraries reside in this directory. Like the LibC library which is used by all binaries. So it is unlikely that you will be able to something.
(If you are lucky and interrupted the command with a quick CTRL+C before is comletion, maybe only sub-dirs are deleted and the LibC is still there)

If the system is totally blocked (login impossible, boot fails, ...), let's hope that you have a Live CD of the same distribution and the same version under the hand.

Boot from this CD, mount the filesystem of your hard-disk and copy the /usr/lib from the Live system to the one on the hard-disk.
ans:
There usually isn’t a direct undo for a safe remove/delete operation on Linux systems, including Raspberry Pi. The closest guidance is to stop using the device as much as possible so you don’t overwrite anything that might still be recoverable.

Then try to restore from:
- a backup
- another copy of the files
- the same live system media, if system files were removed

If system files were deleted and the system is broken, boot from a Live USB/SD with the same Linux version, mount the filesystem, and copy the missing files back from the live system.

q: Use of ./ in running the compiled code
ref:
In Linux, UNIX and related operating systems, . denotes the current directory. Since you want to run a file in your current directory and that directory is not in your $PATH, you need the ./ bit to tell the shell where the executable is. So, ./foo means run the executable called foo that is in this directory.

You can use type or which to get the full path of any commands found in your $PATH.
ans: You need `./` because `.` means the current directory, and programs in the current directory are usually not in your `$PATH`. So `./program` tells the shell to run `program` from here. Commands like `ls` or `gcc` work without `./` because their locations are already in your `$PATH`. If you want to check where a command comes from, use `type` or `which`.

q: Variable Substitution in sed
ref:
You have to use command substitution for this, i.e. instead of

comp={ echo "$fullName" } | sed 's/ //g'

something like

comp=$(echo "$fullName"  | sed 's/ //g')

or

comp=`echo "$fullName"  | sed 's/ //g'`
ans:
To use a shell variable with `sed`’s `s` command, you can capture the `sed` output into another shell variable with command substitution. For example:

comp=$(echo "$fullName" | sed 's/ //g')

or:

comp=`echo "$fullName" | sed 's/ //g'`

This assigns the transformed output to `comp` without extra characters.

q: In bash how can I change the color of my command prompt?
ref:
You'd have to leave a colour trailing after the PS1 (start it after > in your example), and then use the bash DEBUG trap to clear the colour before your command was run (but after you press enter in your shell. Try something like this:

shopt -s extdebug
trap "tput sgr0" DEBUG
ans:
If you mean a bash prompt, put the color in PS1 and reset terminal attributes before the next command runs. For example:

shopt -s extdebug
trap "tput sgr0" DEBUG

This lets the prompt be colored while preventing the typed command from inheriting that color. If you want, I can also help you format a colored PS1 string.

q: What is the difference between $* and $@?
ref:
Using this script:

#! /bin/sh
# Greg Wooledge's args script
printf "%d args:" $#
printf " <%s>" "$@"
echo

Try this demo:

$ set -- a 'b     c' d
$ args $*
4 args: <a> <b> <c> <d>
$ args $@
4 args: <a> <b> <c> <d>
$ args "$*"
1 args: <a b     c d>
$ args "$@"
3 args: <a> <b     c> <d>

You should usually use "$@" (with the quotes).

Sometimes it's useful to change IFS and use "$*":

$ saveIFS=$IFS; IFS='|'; args "$*"; IFS=$saveIFS
1 args: <a|b     c|d>
ans:
Both refer to all positional parameters, but they differ when quoted.

Without quotes, they behave similarly and can split arguments containing spaces.

With quotes:
- "$@" keeps each positional parameter as a separate argument.
- "$*" combines all positional parameters into one single string.

If you want to preserve the original arguments, use "$@".

q: How do I force a user to log out?
ref:
Do you mean you'd like to just automatically boot straight into a system without having to login? That's essentially what they're doing in GParted. You are a user if you go to the terminal and type the command whoami, you are an actual user.

example

                    

You can do this with pretty much any distro. All that's required is to set it up so that it automatically logs in instead of asking you.

See this tutorial on ubuntu.com - AutoLogin

As for elevating this auto logged in user's credentials, again this can be done by adding them to sudo so that they aren't challenged for their password.

See this askubunu question - Execute sudo without Password?. The gist of it is to add the following entry in your sudoer's file (/etc/sudoers):

$ sudo visudo

At the bottom of that file add this line

username ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
ans: The supported guidance here doesn’t provide a way to force a user to log out. It only covers that changes related to a user at login may require logging out and back in, or using auto-login for a graphical session. If your goal is to make a `usermod` change take effect, the closest supported approach is to have the user log out and log back in. If the change is about permissions, make sure the user has the needed sudo access.

q: Keeping a process running on server even SSH is closed
ref:
This only happens if you run ztail (or any other command) as a new root-level process (i.e. without a parent process), e.g. in the background or via cron.

Usually when you start a standard ssh session you get a shell process, which is the root process for all programs you start. If the ssh session terminates, the kernel kills all child processes as well. (That's why people usually use screen or comparable things to retain sessions.)

So the easiest thing for you would be to utilize this default behavior. Have a look at ps axjf to check what ztail's root process is, then figure out why it survives the terminated ssh session.
ans: Start it detached from the SSH session so it is no longer a child of that shell. The supported options mentioned are using a tool like `screen` or launching it as an independent background process. If you start it as part of the SSH shell, it normally ends when the session closes.

q: Alias for redirecting both standard output and standard error, as well as sending to background
ref:
You could make use of the builtin compgen:

compgen: compgen [-abcdefgjksuv] [-o option]  [-A action] [-G globpat]
[-W wordlist]  [-F function] [-C command] [-X filterpat] [-P prefix]
[-S suffix] [word]

    Display possible completions depending on the options.

    Intended to be used from within a shell function generating possible
    completions.  If the optional WORD argument is supplied, matches against
    WORD are generated.

    Exit Status:
    Returns success unless an invalid option is supplied or an error occurs.

TAB at the prompt would list commands, shell builtins, keywords, aliases and functions.  So you could say:

compgen -cbka -A function | grep '^y' > myfile.txt

to get all the options that you see upon typing yTAB at the shell prompt into the file myfile.txt.

Eliminate the grep pipeline in order to get all the possible commands, functions, ... into the file:

compgen -cbka -A function > myfile.txt
ans:
The provided information only shows basic output redirection to a single file, and does not cover redirecting both standard output and standard error, or sending a command to the background. So I can’t confirm an alias for that from the available material.

Closest supported guidance: it demonstrates using `>` to redirect a command’s output to one file, e.g. `compgen -cbka -A function > myfile.txt`.

q: How do I log out/disconnect from SSH after starting a process with output to keep it running?
ref:
Take a look at /proc/PID/fd/ there you can see what happend to your old stdin and stdout. Sometimes you can use echo to send something to the stdin device of that process.

If you just want to prevent commands from being killed after your session breaks you can start them with nohup.

But the best answers to your question are possibly the comments about screen resp. tmux.
ans:
To keep it running after you disconnect, start it with nohup. For example, run:

nohup your_command &

Then log out normally from SSH.

If you need ongoing control or to reconnect later, screen or tmux are better choices. You generally can’t fully reattach control to an arbitrary process from another SSH session; at most, you may be able to inspect its stdin/stdout via /proc/PID/fd.

q: sudo: password prompted even when NOPASSWD is set
ref:
From man sudoers:

   NOPASSWD and PASSWD

   By default, sudo requires that a user authenticate him or herself
   before running a command.  This behavior can be modified via the
   NOPASSWD tag.  Like a Runas_Spec, the NOPASSWD tag sets a default for
   the commands that follow it in the Cmnd_Spec_List.  Conversely, the
   PASSWD tag can be used to reverse things.  For example:

    ray  rushmore = NOPASSWD: /bin/kill, /bin/ls, /usr/bin/lprm

   would allow the user ray to run /bin/kill, /bin/ls, and /usr/bin/lprm
   as root on the machine rushmore without authenticating himself.

One other tag is ALL, to allow the user ray to run any command on any host without password you can use:

ray ALL= NOPASSWD: ALL
ans:
If `NOPASSWD` is set correctly in sudoers, `sudo` should not prompt for a password. The supported configuration is like:

`ray ALL=NOPASSWD: ALL`

This gives user `ray` passwordless sudo for all commands, or you can limit it to specific commands.

If you’re still being prompted, the provided case only confirms that `NOPASSWD` is the right way to disable the prompt; it doesn’t cover other causes of sudo still asking for a password.

q: delete file with name --help.tgz
ref:
You can escape the $ with \:

rm \$file
ans:
Use a form that prevents the name from being treated as an option. For `--help.tgz`, delete it with:

rm -- --help.tgz

You can also quote or prefix the path, for example:

rm './--help.tgz'

The key is to pass the filename as a literal name so `rm` doesn’t interpret it as an option.

q: Why do I have to execute bash programs with ./?
ref:
In Linux, UNIX and related operating systems, . denotes the current directory. Since you want to run a file in your current directory and that directory is not in your $PATH, you need the ./ bit to tell the shell where the executable is. So, ./foo means run the executable called foo that is in this directory.

You can use type or which to get the full path of any commands found in your $PATH.
ans: You need `./` because it tells the shell to run the executable from the current directory. By default, the shell searches only the directories in your PATH, and the current directory is usually not included. So `program` may not be found by name alone, but `./program` explicitly points to the file where you are.

q: Tailing a New File with an Old Name
ans:
If the goal is to keep following a file after it gets renamed, the closest supported approach is to rename files in place while preserving the original name with a fixed prefix. For example:

`for f in *; do mv "$f" "Unix_$f"; done`

This adds `Unix_` to each filename. If you need to act on only some files or include subfolders, a `find`-based loop can be used similarly.

This evidence does not directly address tailing a renamed file, but it does support renaming files while keeping the original name as part of the new name.

q: any way to un-disown / re-attach an interactive process to the tty?
ref:
Yes and no. You can redirect its child's in/out streams - probably your shell - but xterm will have little involvement there. xterm owns the master side of that pty - it does an open on /dev/ptmx and in the process creates /dev/pts/3. But it gives it away - your shell owns that pty now, as xterm makes it the session leader. All xterm does is take the input from the keyboard and pass it to the shell and take output from the shell and pass it to the screen. In this way xterm performs multiplexing functions - subdividing and redirecting input and output between pseudoterminals, but not much else is relevant here once the pty is up.

The virtual consoles, though, are another matter. If your user account is assigned the proper filesystem permissions, you can read them and write to them from other processes - or other terminals - in simpler ways - as in, you needn't pass input/output through a master-side to talk a process running on the slave-side. You can easily do these things in almost every way that matters except where login is concerned. It will kill any listener on that device and will only accept keyboard input. That is its job.

Still, I suspect you're looking for some authentication solution. You can get virtually the same level of security with: 

ssh -t localhost 'exec some process'

That will securely prompt you for authentication then log you into the machine and exec some process in a new pseudoterminal - you can do that from xterm, say.
ans:
Not directly. A terminal emulator like xterm owns its own pseudoterminal and isn’t something you can reattach to as a real tty.

The closest supported approach is to start the process in a new pseudoterminal, for example:

ssh -t localhost 'exec some process'

If you need to interact with a virtual console directly, that may be possible from another process if permissions allow.

q: Undo safely remove device
ref:
I would advise against immediately installing some utility.  Basically your biggest enemy here are disk writes.  You want to avoid them at all costs right now.

Your best bet is an auto-backup created by your editor--if it exists. If not, I would try the following trick using grep if you remember some unique string in your .tex file:

$ sudo grep -i -a -B100 -A100 'string' /dev/sda1 > file.txt

Replace /dev/sda1 with the device that the file was on and replace 'string' with the unique string in your file.  This could take some time.  But basically, what this does is it searches for the string on the device and then returns 100 lines before and after that line  and puts it in file.txt.  If you need more lines returned just adjust the -B and -A options as appropriate.  You might get a bunch of extra garbage returned, but you should be able to get your text back.

Good luck.
ans:
If you mean undoing an accidental removal, the closest supported guidance is to avoid further disk writes as much as possible, because that reduces recovery chances. Don’t install recovery tools right away.

If you only need the content of a text file and remember a unique string from it, you can try searching the device directly and pulling nearby data:

sudo grep -i -a -B100 -A100 'string' /dev/sdX > file.txt

Replace /dev/sdX with the device the file was on. This may include extra garbage, but can sometimes recover text content.

q: How to permanently set environmental variables
ref:
In this specific case, instead of letting Gnome run dbus-launch to create a random D-Bus address, start dbus-daemon explicitly early in your X session startup and give it a fixed address like unix:path=~/.dbus-$HOSTNAME-$DISPLAY.

Given the information in the bug report, you may even be able to get away with unset DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS and let applications find out the bus address from the root window properties.

In the general case, your assessment is correct: all you have is unreliable methods such as ptrace (which may crash the program, or not work due to a security framework such as Apparmor or SELinux) or injecting a shell command (which only works in panes that are currently at a shell prompt). Running a command at each shell prompt (with zsh's preexec or bash's PROMPT_COMMAND) at least doesn't risk breaking stuff.

Another solution would be an LD_PRELOAD library that intercepts getenv calls. This also feels like overkill.

Your best bet is to let the application do the job by creating a level of indirection: arrange for the value of the environment variable to remain valid, and for the application to interpret it in a situation-aware manner. Letting the application look up the D-Bus bus address in the root window properties is an example of this approach.
ans:
To make an environment variable persistent, set it before starting the session or application rather than trying to change it for already-running processes. The supported workaround is to place the setting in your shell startup files or use a shell hook so it’s applied when a new shell session starts. For example, bash can use PROMPT_COMMAND and zsh can use preexec to refresh values at a prompt.

If the variable is for a service like dbus-daemon, the closer supported option is to start it with a fixed address or use an alternate discovery mechanism, since changing it live for running processes is not reliable.

q: How to allow to run su instantly after I added the user to the appropriate group
ref:
I changed /etc/sudoers so that every user that is in the admin group can execute the following commands without being ask for a password.

sudo halt
sudo reboot
sudo poweroff

You just need to add the following lines to /etc/sudoers

## Admin user group is allowed to execute halt and reboot 
%admin ALL=NOPASSWD: /sbin/halt, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/poweroff

and add yourself to the admin group.

If you want only one user to be able to do this just remove the %admin and replace it with username like this

ans:

The provided information does not show a way to make the new group membership apply instantly for `su` without re-login. For immediate access to specific privileged commands, the only example given is using sudoers to allow those commands without a password, but not to refresh group membership in the current session.

q: Find filesystem of an unmounted partition from a script
ref:
How do I tell what sort of data (what data format) is in a file?
→ Use the file utility.

Here, you want to know the format of data in a device file, so you need to pass the -s flag to tell file not just to say that it's a device file but look at the content. Sometimes you'll need the -L flag as well, if the device file name is a symbolic link. You'll see output like this:

# file -sL /dev/sd*
/dev/sda1: Linux rev 1.0 ext4 filesystem data, UUID=63fa0104-4aab-4dc8-a50d-e2c1bf0fb188 (extents) (large files) (huge files)
/dev/sdb1: Linux rev 1.0 ext2 filesystem data, UUID=b3c82023-78e1-4ad4-b6e0-62355b272166
/dev/sdb2: Linux/i386 swap file (new style), version 1 (4K pages), size 4194303 pages, no label, UUID=3f64308c-19db-4da5-a9a0-db4d7defb80f

Given this sample output, the first disk has one partition and the second disk has two partitions. /dev/sda1 is an ext4 filesystem, /dev/sdb1 is an ext2 filesystem, and /dev/sdb2 is some swap space (about 4GB).

You must run this command as root, because ordinary users may not read disk partitions directly: if needed, add sudo in front.
ans:
Use `file` with `-s` so it inspects the device contents, and `-L` if the device path is a symlink. For example:

`sudo file -sL /dev/sdb1`

For a script, run it on the specific partition device name you want to inspect, such as `/dev/sdb1` or `/dev/sdb2`. It can report filesystems like `ext2/ext4` or `swap`. Root privileges may be needed to read the partition directly.

q: is there a way to keep a session alive even when logging out?
ref:
This is a bit of a hack but you could add this to your interactive shell configuration:

alias tmuxn='tmux new-session -s $$'

ans:

q: Remove accidentally extracted files
ref:
If you delete /usr/lib, you will kill your system as very crucial libraries reside in this directory. Like the LibC library which is used by all binaries. So it is unlikely that you will be able to something.

q: I ran rm -rf. Need to recover files
ref:
MacOS is a Unix OS and rm means "good-bye". The GUI interface allows you to move a file to the trash (which you can then recover) but that's not what you did.  If you have a backup (e.g. you have Time Machine running) then you are saved.

Clarification

Strictly speaking (as @ire_and_curses points out) a rm simply deletes the directory entry for the file while leaving the disk blocks it used, untouched.  If you could quiesce the filesystem in which the file had been, there are advanced methods by which you can try to re-discover those blocks contents.  There are also some recovery tools which can be purchased to recover the loss.  The central issue is that nothing else re-uses any of the disk blocks represented by your file.

The MacOS also has a secure remove command (srm) which over-writes a file before it is unlinked making it unrecoverable.  I use the unlink term since this is the underlying system call associated with a shell's rm command.  This sets the stage for the next part of this discussion, below.

Sidenote

[ I should hasten to add that even if you over-write a disk multiple times, there are ways to read what was written a dozen or more times before.  To properly sanitize a disk for disposal really requires an acid bath, a big hammer and a shredder. ]

unlinking a file decrements the file's inode link-count.  If this value reaches zero, the file is deleted from the filesystem directory and its disk blocks freed for re-use.  This only happens when no processes hav
ans:
If the files were deleted with `rm -rf`, there is no simple terminal undo. The best options are:

- Restore from a backup, if you have one.
- Try file recovery tools, but success depends on whether the disk blocks have been reused.
- Stop using the drive as much as possible to avoid overwriting the deleted data.

Recovery may still be possible if the data blocks are intact and not reused, but `rm` removes the file’s directory entry, so there’s no built-in restore.

q: Why is some filesystem space used even though the filesystem is empty?
ref:
du == Disk Usage. It walks through directory tree and counts the sum size of all files therein. It may not output exact information due to the possibility of unreadable files, hardlinks in directory tree, etc. It will show information about the specific directory requested. Think, "How much disk space is being used by these files?"

df == Disk Free. Looks at disk used blocks directly in filesystem metadata. Because of this it returns much faster that du but can only show info about the entire disk/partition. Think, "How much free disk space do I have?"
ans: Because `df` and `du` measure different things. `du` only totals files visible in the directory tree you check, while `df` shows used blocks for the whole filesystem or partition. So even if a filesystem looks empty, `df` can still report space as used because it includes filesystem-level block usage that `du` does not see.

q: Correctly determining memory usage in Linux
ref:
Linux uses RAM in a different way from what other operating systems do.

Rather than sitting there with unused RAM, Linux stores data that it thinks might be used in RAM-any applications may be cached here, files, etc.

As a result, Linux RAM usage is higher than what is used by running applications. This extra usage is buffered to be sued by other things. Run free -h and the second row under used will show you that a lot of the "used" memory is really just cached.

In the case where all of your memory is cached and a program needs memory, it will remove enough from the cache to fit that program.
ans: The memory shown as “used” by `top` or `free` is not necessarily lost. Linux uses RAM for cache and buffers, so usage can look high even with no active applications. This cached memory is normally reclaimed automatically when programs need RAM, so you usually do not need to reboot. The `-/+ buffers/cache` line in `free` shows how much of the apparent usage is actually reusable cache. After a reboot, that cache is cleared, which is why usage drops.

q: How do I rename multiple files
ref:
You can use rename to rename files based on a pattern, and one of the examples from the man page is changing the extension of a group of files. It takes the source pattern, modified pattern, and the files to operate on, so in your case:

$ rename .x .y *.x

It changes the first occurrence of .x to .y, so if you happen to have .x anywhere other than the end of the filename it's going to change that first
ans:
To rename multiple files by changing an extension, use:

`rename .x .y *.x`

This replaces the first occurrence of `.x` with `.y` for each file matching `*.x`. If `.x` appears elsewhere in the filename, that first occurrence is what gets changed, so use it carefully.

q: Unix filesys reserved space
ref:
A common programming technique is to create a temporary file and immediately unlink() it. This leaves the file (and its space) available for the duration of the program but automatically causes its removal when the program using it terminates. One advantage is that no epilog (cleanup) code is necessary to write.

To determine if you have a process holding an unlinked file open, do:

lsof -a +L1 /dev/server_slash

(or)

lsof +D /dev/server_slash +L1

Look for any files with an NLINK value of zero (0). These would be files with a zero link count that will vanish when the last process terminates. The SIZE/OFFSET column will offer the character size of the file in question.
ans:
If disk space is showing as used but not reflected by `du`, the supported explanation here is that the space may belong to a deleted/unlinked file that is still open by a running process. In that case, `du` won’t count it, but `df` will.

You can check for these with:

`lsof -a +L1 /`

or

`lsof +D / +L1`

Look for entries with `NLINK` 0. The space is freed only when the process closes the file or exits.

q: Why is learning command line imporatant?
ref:
There is no universal answer here....as the output from a given command is the responsibility of the author of that particular program not anything in the Linux operating system or any of the shells.  In general, I try to use --help and hope for the best, but in cases of filter type programs, you might not get anything at all.  

Assumming the man pages are installed, they are one of the best sources for command line information.....otherthan the source code itself.

ans: Learning the command line is important because it gives you direct access to many program features and documentation tools. Learning it helps you find and use the right documentation for each command and work more efficiently.

q: Accidently created a file called -X, how can I delete it?
ref:
Debian

If you're using a Debian based distro then this is likely what's causing your issue.

motd - Debian Wiki

excerpt

  /etc/motd in Debian

  
  Debian has a peculiar way of handling /etc/motd. The motd is updated at every reboot, in a boot script (/etc/init.d/bootmisc.sh in lenny and below, /etc/init.d/bootlogs in squeeze and above), which basically runs the following:

   uname -snrvm > /var/run/motd
   [ -f /etc/motd.tail ] && cat /etc/motd.tail >> /var/run/motd

  
  Since /etc/motd is a symlink to /var/run/motd in Debian, this works.

  
  How to update your /etc/motd

  
  Since /etc/motd basically gets overwritten at every reboot, you need to instead update /etc/motd.tail and either reboot (!!) or also edit /etc/motd.tail or run the above commands. There is a bug report (437176) to provide an easier command to allow you to update only /etc/motd.tail.

Red Hat based distros (Fedora/CentOS/RHEL)

For these types of distros I'm not aware of any automated system that would revert these files back to known versions as part of a reboot. These files are often times statically included on these systems in RPM packages such as these:

CentOS 5.x

$ rpm -qf /etc/issue /etc/motd
centos-release-5-9.el5.centos.1
setup-2.5.58-9.el5

CentOS 6.x

$ rpm -qf /etc/issue /etc/motd 
centos-release-6-5.el6.centos.11.2.x86_64
setup-2.8.14-20.el6_4.1.noarch

Fedora 19

$ rpm -qf /etc/issue /etc/motd 
fedora-release-19-8.noarch
setup-2.8.71-1.fc19.noarch

Further more a simple search for
ans:
If the filename starts with a dash, use `--` to stop option parsing. For example:

`rm -- -X`

You can also use the full path:

`rm -- ./-X`

This supported guidance only covers deletion of a file named `-X`; if you meant a different path or issue, it doesn’t cover that.

q: "tail -f" show old file after file has been rotated
ref:
Using the perl script prename, which is symlinked to rename on Debian based distros.

rename -n 's/^([^_]*)_.*/$1.txt/' *_*.txt

Remove the -n once you are sure it does what you want.
ans:
`tail -f` can keep showing the old file descriptor after rotation, so it may not follow the newly created file with the same name. The better choice is:

tail -F filename

This follows the filename across rotations or replacements, so when the old file is renamed and a new one appears, it keeps tracking the new file. If you use `tail -f`, it may continue reading the original file instead.

q: Rename files in directory
ref:
You can use this command :

for folder in $(ls); do
    for file in $(ls $folder); do
        sed -i 's/_b//' $folder/$file
    done
    mv $folder ${folder/_b/}
done

First loop is browsing directories.

Second loop is editing contents of files located in folders.

After leaving second loop, first one is renaming folders.

Another way for dealing with spaces in filenames which would be interpreted as IFS :

ls | while read folder ; do
 ls "$folder" | while read file; do
  sed -i 's/_b//' "$folder/$file"
 done
 mv "$folder" "${folder/_b/}"
done
ans:
You can rename files in a directory by looping over the filenames and using `mv` with a modified name. A similar pattern is:

for file in /path/to/dir/*; do
  mv "$file" "${file/_b/}"
done

This supports renaming by substituting part of the name, such as removing `_b` from filenames. If filenames may contain spaces, avoid using plain `ls` and use a safer loop. It does not cover arbitrary renaming rules.

q: How can I identify the variant of Unix/Linux from a shell?
ref:
Several ways, from most to least reliable (and most-to-least "heavy"):

ps -p$$ -ocmd=.  (On Solaris, this may need to be ps -p$$ -ofname= and on macOS and on BSD should be ps -p$$ -ocommand=.)

Check for $BASH_VERSION, $ZSH_VERSION, and other shell-specific variables.

Check $SHELL; this is a last resort, as it specifies your default shell and not necessarily the current shell.
ans:
From a shell, the supported check here is to inspect the parent init process:

```bash
ps -p 1 -o comm=
```

If it prints `systemd`, the system is using systemd; if it prints `init`, it’s likely SysV init.

This helps identify the init system/Unix-Linux variant in a limited way, but the provided information does not give a general command for fully identifying the OS variant from a shell.

q: SSH: connect through intermediary server in just one step (through forwarded port)
ref:
Master connection

It's easiest if you plan in advance.

Open a master connection the first time. For subsequent connections, route slave connections through the existing master connection. In your ~/.ssh/config, set up connection sharing to happen automatically:

ControlMaster auto
ControlPath ~/.ssh/control:%h:%p:%r

If you start an ssh session to the same (user, port, machine) as an existing connection, the second session will be tunneled over the first. Establishing the second connection requires no new authentication and is very fast.

So while you have your active connection, you can quickly:

copy a file with scp or rsync;

mount a remote filesystem with sshfs.

Forwarding

On an existing connection, you can establish a reverse ssh tunnel. On the ssh command line, create a remote forwarding by passing -R 22042:localhost:22 where 22042 is a randomly chosen number that's different from any other port number on the remote machine. Then ssh -p 22042 localhost on the remote machine connects you back to the source machine; you can use scp -P 22042 foo localhost: to copy files.

You can automate this further with RemoteForward 22042 localhost:22. The problem with this is that if you connect to the same computer with multiple instances of ssh, or if someone else is using the port, you don't get the forwarding.

If you haven't enabled a remote forwarding from the start, you can do it on an existing ssh session. Type Enter ~C Enter -R 22042:localhost:22 Enter.
See “Escape charac
ans:
Yes. If you already have an SSH session open, the supported way is to add a reverse tunnel back to your local machine. That exposes a local service on the remote side via a remote localhost port, so you can reach it through the SSH connection in one step.

The same approach applies to SSH or other services: forward a remote port to a local port, then connect to `localhost` on the remote machine using that forwarded port.

If the session is already open, you can add the forwarding with the SSH escape sequence `~C` and a `-R` rule.

q: Bash alias arguments
ref:
Aliases are like commands in that all arguments to them are passed as arguments to the program they alias. For instance:

alias ls='ls -l -a -t -r'
# This now executes 'ls -l -a -t -r foo bar'
ls foo bar

If you want to have actual control over how the arguments are interpreted, then you could write a function like so:

my_program_wrapper() {
    local first_arg=$1 \
          second_arg=$2

    shift 2 # get rid of the first two arguments

    # ...

    /path/to/my_program "$@"
}
ans: An alias doesn’t take ownership of an argument or “use it up.” Arguments typed after the alias are passed to the command it expands to, so they’re still available to that command each time you use the alias. If you need to transform, reorder, or otherwise handle arguments more flexibly, a shell function is the better choice.

q: Why do I get "Permission denied" when redirecting the output of sudo echo "xyz" to a file?
ref:
It is normal. The file after the > is not open by the process running under sudo, but by the shell, which isn't. Try this instead:

printf "foo" | sudo tee /etc/file
ans:
Because `>` is handled by your shell, not by `sudo`. So in `sudo echo "xyz" > file`, `sudo` only applies to `echo`; the shell still tries to open the file itself, using your normal permissions, and gets “Permission denied.”

To write to a file that needs elevated access, run the writing command under `sudo`, for example:

`printf "xyz" | sudo tee /path/to/file`

That lets `tee` open the file with the needed permissions.

q: How do I use redirection with sudo
ref:
When working on a command line the shell first does the redirections and after that does the execve to the external command. This means that the redirections are performed with unchanged user rights (because the shell doesn't care about sudo getting involved later).

The sudo command which could easily do >> results.txt doesn't see that but just gets a changed file descriptor for /dev/stdout.

Two possibilities:

You make the redirection to a file / directory which is writable to you (User2).

You write a wrapper script which does that and call the wrapper script via sudo.
ans:
`sudo` only elevates the command it runs; the shell handles `>` or `>>` first, using your normal user permissions. So `sudo command > file` can fail even though `command` ran as root.

To make the redirection use elevated permissions, either:
- redirect to a file you already have access to,
- run a shell with `sudo` and put the redirection inside it, or
- use a wrapper script that does the redirection with the needed privileges.

q: How do I log out/disconnect from SSH after starting a process with output to keep it running?
ref:
Take a look at /proc/PID/fd/ there you can see what happend to your old stdin and stdout. Sometimes you can use echo to send something to the stdin device of that process.

If you just want to prevent commands from being killed after your session breaks you can start them with nohup.

But the best answers to your question are possibly the comments about screen resp. tmux.
ans:
If your goal is to keep a process running after you disconnect SSH, start it with nohup. For future interactive control, screen or tmux are the better tools.

There isn’t a general way to fully reattach control of an arbitrary running process from another SSH session. You may be able to inspect a process’s stdin/stdout via /proc/PID/fd and sometimes send input to its stdin device with echo, but that’s limited.

q: How to forward X over SSH from Ubuntu machine?
ref:
If you run ssh with X forwarding, this is transparent: remote commands (including xclip) have access to your X server (including its keyboard). Make sure you have ForwardX11 yes in your ~/.ssh/config and X11Forwarding yes in the server sshd_config (depending on your distributions, these options may be on or off by default).

<myconffile.conf sed {...} | xclip -i

There are other ways of working on remote files that may be more convenient, for example mounting remote directories on your local machine with SSHfs, or opening remote files in Emacs with Tramp. If you have ssh and FUSE set up and SSHfs installed, SSHfs is as easy as mkdir ~/net/myserver; sshfs myserver:/ ~/net/myserver. If you have ssh set up and Emacs installed, Tramp is as easy as opening /myserver:/path/to/file.
ans:
Use SSH with X forwarding. On your Ubuntu client, enable `ForwardX11 yes` in `~/.ssh/config`. On the SSH server, ensure `X11Forwarding yes` is set in `sshd_config`.

Then connect normally and run the X command on the remote machine, for example:

`xrandr ...`

With X forwarding enabled, remote GUI/X commands can use your local X server. If X forwarding isn’t available, the only nearby alternatives mentioned are SSHfs or Emacs Tramp, but they won’t give `xrandr` access.

The above command will retain Uppercase,lowercase letters ,underscore and numbers. It removes all other chars.

Replace `-x` with the exact string you want removed. If the string is at a particular position, the same substitution approach applies as long as you match the exact text you want deleted.

q: Rename file in another directory without repeating path
ref:
You can use this command :

for folder in $(ls); do
    for file in $(ls $folder); do
        sed -i 's/_b//' $folder/$file
    done
    mv $folder ${folder/_b/}
done

First loop is browsing directories.

Second loop is editing contents of files located in folders.

After leaving second loop, first one is renaming folders.

Another way for dealing with spaces in filenames which would be interpreted as IFS :

ls | while read folder ; do
 ls "$folder" | while read file; do
  sed -i 's/_b//' "$folder/$file"
 done
 mv "$folder" "${folder/_b/}"
done
ans:
You can use the same `mv` pattern and build the new name from the existing path. For example, to rename files in another directory without repeating the full path in the destination:

for file in /path/to/dir/*; do
  mv "$file" "${file/_b/}"
done

If the rename is just changing part of the filename, this works directly. If you mean renaming within a different directory, use the full source path in the loop and only transform the filename portion in the destination. This does not cover arbitrary renaming rules.

q: How to rename multiple files
ref:
You can use rename to rename files based on a pattern, and one of the examples from the man page is changing the extension of a group of files. It takes the source pattern, modified pattern, and the files to operate on, so in your case:

$ rename .x .y *.x

It changes the first occurrence of .x to .y, so if you happen to have .x anywhere other than the end of the filename it's going to change that first
ans:
Use `rename` on all matching files. To change an extension across multiple files:

`rename .x .y *.x`

This replaces the first occurrence of `.x` with `.y` in each matching filename.

To remove an extension instead, use the same approach but replace it with nothing:

`rename .x '' *.x`

This is the closest supported pattern for bulk renaming by removing the extension.

do    
 echo $name
 var=$var$name //$ should be removed which is prefixed before var. Blank space before and after equal sign should be removed to run this code.

q: man pages: meaning of '2' in STAT(2)?
ref:
The number corresponds to what section of the manual that page is from; 1 is user commands, while 8 is sysadmin stuff. The man page for man itself (man man) explains it and lists the standard ones:

MANUAL SECTIONS
    The standard sections of the manual include:

    1      User Commands
    2      System Calls
    3      C Library Functions
    4      Devices and Special Files
    5      File Formats and Conventions
    6      Games et. al.
    7      Miscellanea
    8      System Administration tools and Daemons

    Distributions customize the manual section to their specifics,
    which often include additional sections.

There are certain terms that have different pages in different sections (e.g. printf as a command appears in section 1, as a stdlib function appears in section 3); in cases like that you can pass the section number to man before the page name to choose which one you want, or use man -a to show every matching page in a row:

$ man 1 printf
$ man 3 printf
$ man -a printf

You can tell what sections a term falls in with man -k (equivalent to the apropos command). It will do substring matches too (e.g. it will show sprintf if you run man -k printf), so you need to use ^term to limit it:

$ man -k '^printf'
printf               (1)  - format and print data
printf               (1p)  - write formatted output
printf               (3)  - formatted output conversion
printf               (3p)  - print formatted output
printf [builtins]    (1)  - bash built-in com
ans: The “2” means the man page is in section 2 of the manual. Section numbers identify the page’s category. In the standard layout, section 1 is user commands, section 3 is library functions, and section 8 is system administration tools and daemons. If a name appears in multiple sections, you can specify one with something like `man 2 name` or use `man -a name` to see all matches.

q: where should I put the sudo in this command?
ref:
You can't just stick sudo in front of a shell command, you have to invoke a shell to evaluate that command again (doing things like expanding variables, opening files for redirection operators, etc.). So that's

sudo bash -c !!

except that this doesn't quite work, because !! interpolates the text of the previous command, special characters and all. You need to retrieve the text of the command as a string and pass that as an argument to sh. Fortunately, bash's fc builtin lets you do that¹.

sudo bash -c "$(fc -ln -1)"

Or even, to be sure to invoke the same version of bash that's currently running:

sudo "$BASH" -c "$(fc -ln -1)"

Note that since the command is executed in a separate shell process, it inherits environment variables (only the ones that sudo preserves, mind), but not shell internal variables. Shell options (e.g. kshglob) and other settings will start from the default either.

The same command² works in zsh and ksh, though ATT ksh93 requires both the first and last number to be passed to fc³ (which also works in bash, zsh and pdksh/mksh):

sudo zsh -c "$(fc -ln -1)"
sudo ksh -c "$(fc -ln -1 -1)"
sudo "$0" -c "$(fc -ln -1 -1)"

Using $0 to designate the executable of the running shell works only if the shell was invoked through the $PATH and the $PATH hasn't changed, or through an absolute path.

Here's another method in zsh which is slightly clearer but longer:

sudo zsh -c $history[$[HISTCMD-1]]

A final word of warning: sudo is for potentially dangerous comman
ans:
Put `sudo` before the shell that performs the redirection, not just before the command.

For example:
`sudo bash -c 'command > /path/file'`

Or, if you want to use your current Bash:
`sudo "$BASH" -c 'command > /path/file'`

For simple writes to a root-owned file, you can also use:
`echo "something" | sudo tee /path/foobar`

q: undelete files from local fileserver
ref:
If you delete /usr/lib, you will kill your system as very crucial libraries reside in this directory. Like the LibC library which is used by all binaries. So it is unlikely that you will be able to something.
(If you are lucky and interrupted the command with a quick CTRL+C before is comletion, maybe only sub-dirs are deleted and the LibC is still there)

If the system is totally blocked (login impossible, boot fails, ...), let's hope that you have a Live CD of the same distribution and the same version under the hand.

Boot from this CD, mount the filesystem of your hard-disk and copy the /usr/lib from the Live system to the one on the hard-disk.
ans:

If only some subdirectories were deleted and you interrupted it quickly, the system may still partly work, but recovery still depends on restoring the missing files from backup or another source.

q: Linux From Scratch: make no such file or directory, bad interpreter
ref:
This kind of message is usually due to a buggy shebang line, either an extra carriage return at the end of the first line or a BOM at the beginning of it.

Run:

$ head -1 yourscript | od -c

and see how it ends.

This is wrong:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n

This is wrong too:

0000000 357 273 277   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

This is correct:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

Use dos2unix (or sed, tr, awk, perl, python…) to fix your script if this is the issue.

Here is one that will remove both of a BOM and tailing CRs:

sed -i '1s/^.*#//;s/\r$//' brokenScript

Note that the shell you are using to run the script will slightly affect the error messages that are displayed.
Here are three scripts just showing their name (echo $0) and having the following respective shebang lines:

correctScript:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

scriptWithBom:

0000000 357 273 277   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \n

scriptWithCRLF:

0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n

Under bash, running them will show these messages:

$ ./correctScript
./correctScript
$ ./scriptWithCRLF
bash: ./scriptWithCRLF: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
$ ./scriptWithBom
./scriptWithBom: line 1: #!/bin/bash: No such file or directory
./scriptWithBom

Running the buggy ones by explicitely calling the interpreter allows the CRLF script to run without any issue:

$
ans:
Use a normal shebang with env, like:

`#!/usr/bin/env sed -f`

If you get “No such file or directory” or “bad interpreter,” the likely problem is the first line format, often Windows CRLF line endings or a BOM. Check it with:

`head -1 yourscript | od -c`

It should end with `\n`, not `\r\n`. If needed, convert the file to Unix format:

`dos2unix script.sh`

or:

`sed -i 's/\r$//' script.sh`

Then try again.

q: -exec isn't being passed all the files found by find
ans:
`find` does not pass a shell-expanded command to `-exec`; it replaces `{}` itself with matched paths.

Use:

`find . -type f -exec grep -l strings {} \;`

`-exec '{}'` is not the normal form. Quoting `{}` makes it a literal argument, not the placeholder `find` expects.

So if it seems like not all files are being passed, the supported syntax is still `... -exec command {} \;`.
