q: SSH: connect through intermediary server in just one step (through forwarded port)
ref:
In /etc/ssh/sshd for Computer B set:

AllowTcpForwarding yes
TCPKeepAlive yes

From Computer A:

$ ssh -R 2222:localhost:22 ip.of.computer.b

From Computer B:

$ ssh localhost -p 2222

Note that 2222 is an arbitrary high-port number I picked. That port on Computer B will then be tunneled back through the SSH connection initialized on Computer A to port 22. If you have multiple machines you should use a different port for each machine.

For your use case you will probably want to run this from a script so that you can make it a daemon and periodically try to re-connect if the link is dropped. You will probably want a special account with a shell of just /bin/true on Computer B to handle the incoming connections. You can then setup either a single key or multiple keys for each machine that are allowed to "call home".

On Computer A you might find the -n, -N and -T options useful to disconnect it from local input (so it can run in the background), not try to run any remote command, just open the tunnel, and not create a tty.

Most normal methods of spawning a daemon don't work very well with setting up a network tunnel like this. A problem in network connectivity would make it try to beat the wall down to get through. A simple loop with a sleep to wait should do the trick. Ten minutes is a nice number because it doesn't flood the network and log files with attemps if there is a problem (like Computer B being offline) but it still gets you back in reasonably quick if the connecti
ans:
Yes—use reverse SSH tunneling.

On the machine behind the intermediary/router, open an SSH session outward with a reverse port forward, for example:

ssh -R 2222:localhost:22 yourcomputer

Then, from the other side, connect to the forwarded port:

ssh localhost -p 2222

This gives you one-step access through the intermediary. It requires SSH server settings that allow TCP forwarding. If the connection may drop, run the client-side SSH command from a script or daemon so it reconnects automatically. If you need multiple LAN machines, use a different high port for each one.

You use that to refer to jobs:

refers to any job of which the command line contains the character string abc.

q: Is there a way to refer to multiple files in a directory without retyping the whole path?
ans:
Yes. If you’re already in the directory, you can refer to multiple files without retyping the full path by using a shell loop over `*`:

`for f in *; do mv "$f" "Unix_$f"; done`

q: What's the difference of get command output using`command`and $(command) in Shell?
ref:
This isn't a command itself, rather this is an example of command substitution. It takes the value of what is in parentheses and uses it in context.

For example, I will frequently make a backup of a file before editing it. I'll use command substitution to add the date to the end of the filename in ISO 8601 format (for sorting.) Of course, I could just type the date, but this is great for scripts where the date may be different each time it runs.

$ cp -p /path/to/file /path/to/file.$(date +%F)
$ ls /path/to/file.*
/path/to/file.2013-09-10 /path/to/file
ans:
`command` just runs the command normally.

`$(command)` is command substitution: the shell runs `command` and replaces `$(command)` with whatever it prints.

So if you want the output as text inside another command or in a variable, use `$(...)`. If you just want it executed for its normal effect, use `command`.

q: `du -sh` reports different used size than `df -h`
ref:
du == Disk Usage. It walks through directory tree and counts the sum size of all files therein. It may not output exact information due to the possibility of unreadable files, hardlinks in directory tree, etc. It will show information about the specific directory requested. Think, "How much disk space is being used by these files?"

df == Disk Free. Looks at disk used blocks directly in filesystem metadata. Because of this it returns much faster that du but can only show info about the entire disk/partition. Think, "How much free disk space do I have?"
ans:
`du` and `df` measure different things.

`du -sh` totals the files it can see under the directory you point it at. `df -h` reports used blocks for the whole filesystem or partition.

So if `df` shows more used space than `du`, the extra space is likely usage not included in that directory tree view, because `df` reflects the filesystem’s actual block usage.

chsh -s /bin/ksh

rahmu:x:1000:1000:My Nameisrahmu,,,:/home/rahmu:/bin/bash

q: How does the syntax "${foo##*.}" work to get file extensions?
ref:
Interpretation of *.* under old Windows/DOS systems

The significance here is more related to Windows/DOS than to Unix/Linux. On old Windows/DOS systems it was a 'wildcard' pattern. Wildcard patterns were used for matching filenames in a similar manner to Unix globs. The *.* wildcard was commonly used to match any file.

As with a Unix glob, the * will match any sequence of characters in a filename, as such * on its own will also match any file. However the reason why *.* will match any filename too is due to differences in the way that these wildcards work. According to this article:

Any characters other than a dot that come after an asterisk have no effect, since the asterisk moves the cursor to position 12, at which point nothing changes the parse state except for a dot, which clears the last three positions and moves the cursor.

This behaviour (somewhat odd from Unix perspective) means that a dot following a * does not actually match a dot, but is just a hackish way to allow you to add more characters to the pattern. This means that adding another * will match anything in these last three positions.

This makes a little more sense when you consider that the syntax was used on DOS and old Windows systems before Windows 95 which required 8.3 filenames. These filenames were only allowed to have one dot and at most three characters following the dot. Most, if not all files on the system would have a three character extension (even though technically a shorter or no extensio
ans:
The syntax `${foo##*.}` is shell parameter expansion, but the provided information does not fully explain it.

The closest supported guidance is that `*` can act as a wildcard matching any characters. In `${foo##*.}`, the `*.`
pattern is used to match everything up to the last dot, so the result is the part after that dot, which is commonly the file extension.

However, the evidence does not confirm the exact behavior of `##` or `%` in shell parameter expansion, so I can’t fully verify the syntax from what’s given.

q: Recover deleted files on Raspberry Pi?
ref:
MacOS is a Unix OS and rm means "good-bye". The GUI interface allows you to move a file to the trash (which you can then recover) but that's not what you did.  If you have a backup (e.g. you have Time Machine running) then you are saved.

Clarification

Strictly speaking (as @ire_and_curses points out) a rm simply deletes the directory entry for the file while leaving the disk blocks it used, untouched.  If you could quiesce the filesystem in which the file had been, there are advanced methods by which you can try to re-discover those blocks contents.  There are also some recovery tools which can be purchased to recover the loss.  The central issue is that nothing else re-uses any of the disk blocks represented by your file.

The MacOS also has a secure remove command (srm) which over-writes a file before it is unlinked making it unrecoverable.  I use the unlink term since this is the underlying system call associated with a shell's rm command.  This sets the stage for the next part of this discussion, below.

Sidenote

[ I should hasten to add that even if you over-write a disk multiple times, there are ways to read what was written a dozen or more times before.  To properly sanitize a disk for disposal really requires an acid bath, a big hammer and a shredder. ]

unlinking a file decrements the file's inode link-count.  If this value reaches zero, the file is deleted from the filesystem directory and its disk blocks freed for re-use.  This only happens when no processes hav
ans:
If the files were deleted with `rm` on Raspberry Pi/Linux, they’re usually gone from the filesystem, not sent to Trash. The only certain way to get them back is from a backup.

If you don’t have a backup, recovery may still be possible with data recovery tools, but it depends on whether the disk blocks have been reused. To improve the chance:
- stop using the drive immediately
- avoid writing any new data to it
- try recovery tools or a recovery service as soon as possible

The more you use the drive, the lower the chance of recovery.

df == Disk Free. Looks at disk used blocks directly in filesystem metadata. Because of this it returns much faster that du but can only show info about the entire disk/partition. Think, "How much free disk space do I have?"

q: Why do you need the "./" when executing programs in the current directory?
ref:
In Linux, UNIX and related operating systems, . denotes the current directory. Since you want to run a file in your current directory and that directory is not in your $PATH, you need the ./ bit to tell the shell where the executable is. So, ./foo means run the executable called foo that is in this directory.

You can use type or which to get the full path of any commands found in your $PATH.
ans: `./` tells the shell to run the program from the current directory. Without it, the shell searches the directories in `$PATH`, and the current directory is usually not included. So if your compiled program is in the folder you’re currently in, `./yourprogram` runs that exact file. Built-in or installed commands like `ls` or `gcc` don’t need `./` because the shell finds them through `$PATH`.

q: cycle through one command's output and use in another command
ref:
(This refers to bash in case of doubt)

The output of one command or one pipeline can be made the input of another command by creating a (or extending the existing) pipeline:

command1 | command2
command1 | command2 | command3

Several commands (including pipelines) can be combined with a subshell or a list (group command). This combination becomes the first part of the pipeline then:

(command1; command2 | command3; command4) | command5
{command1; command2 | command3; command4;} | command5 # note the ; before }

Another possibility is a "here string" (or even a "here document"):

command2 <<< $(command1)

command2 <<EOT
First input line
$(command1)
Last input line
EOT

Other cases

Command substitution is used when the output shall be part of a command line i.e. if one command shall see the output of another as its own parameter:

echo $(date)

echo sees the output of date as its parameter; as if it had been typed in the command line.

Process substitution makes the output of another process appearing as the content of a (non-seekable) file given as parameter on the command line.

grep bar <(echo $'foo\nbar\nbaz')

looks to grep like

echo $'foo\nbar\nbaz' > /path/to/file
grep bar /path/to/file
ans:
The supported pattern here is piping one command’s output into another command, like:

`command1 | command2`

If you mean “use the output from one command repeatedly as input to another,” that specific looping behavior isn’t covered by the evidence. It only shows piping, grouping multiple commands before a pipe, command substitution, and process substitution.

If you want to chain commands, the closest supported forms are:

`(command1; command2 | command3; command4) | command5`

or

`{ command1; command2 | command3; command4; } | command5`

q: How to hide “all traffic” when plotting rows in Google Analytics?
ref:
This graph is available in Google Analytics but getting it is not easy.  You don't need to use advanced segments for it though.  I figured this out for a similar problem which I blogged about: Graphing the performance of sub-domains.   I also wrote a similar answer to In Google Analytics, how can I graph direct traffic vs Google referrals?  Here are the steps you need to follow:

Select the date range you want.

Navigate to "Traffic Sources" -> "Sources" -> "Referrals"

Change the number of results per page to enough so that the ones you want to compare are all on the first page of results.

Click on the "Motion Charts" icon (it is three black dots located top right of the graph).  I don't know why some line graphs are hidden under motion charts, it doesn't make sense to me.

On the left of the graph change the sideways select from "Pages/Visit" to "Visits"

Click the tab icon on the top of graph that has a line on it (there is another line graph icon next to the motion charts icon, but you don't want that one)

Use the check boxes to the right of the graph to select the referrers that you want to compare.
ans:
You can’t just hide the “all traffic” line in the regular plot-rows view. The closest workaround is to use the Motion Charts view instead:

Select your date range.
Go to Traffic Sources > Sources > Referrals.
Make sure the referrers you want are on the first page.
Click the Motion Charts icon (three black dots at the top right of the graph).
Change the metric on the left to Visits.
Then switch to the line-chart tab and use the checkboxes to select only the referrers you want.

That gives you a comparison graph without the oversized “all traffic” line dominating the chart.

q: Is it a bad idea for my homepage to be in a sub-folder?
ref:
The problem you're facing is two sided:

SEO-wise: pages that are closest to the root are generally seen by search engines as most important. Therefor I would strongly suggest you use the full domainname (e.g. www.domainname.com) as the homepage. If the website has a lot of subdirectories these are placed one level down in the website by default. You would want to keep the amount of subsequent directories to a minimum. On top of that: as Lese states: if you want to change the folder in the future and everyone has linked to www.domainname.com/folder instead of www.domainname.com you need to create 301-redirects for those links to save the link juice.

User experience: it's kind of shady, especially for a large educational institution to open in a folder. Back in 2000 it wouldn't be a problem, but with the current user's expectations and experience I would strongly suggest to open the homepage at the root from a user perspective as well.
ans:
Yes, it’s generally better not to have the homepage only in a sub-folder. The accepted guidance says pages closest to the root are usually seen as most important by search engines, so using the full domain as the homepage is preferred. It also notes that if you later move the site, links pointing to /folder would need 301 redirects to preserve link value.

From a user-experience perspective, opening the site in a folder was described as “kind of shady” and less aligned with current expectations.

So the closest supported advice is: keep the homepage at the root if possible, and use subfolders for sections beneath it.

q: SSL Hosting Support for site with existing SSL certificate
ref:
Certificates are priced and issued depending on your need. Lower end certificates are good for simply providing an encrypted connection for your visitors, useful when you collect personally identifiable information that is not financially related. The verification process to get one of these is usually very simple:

The certificate company looks up the contact e-mail for your domain (via whois)

The certificate company sends you an e-mail to verify the SSL request

You verify the request and they deliver your cert shortly after

If your site is e-commerce related, where users have to put in credit card / bank information to complete transactions (even if you don't store it, which I hope you would not), the certificate needs to do more than just encrypt the connection, it needs to verify the identity of your company. These certificates are of a higher grade, and require more work to verify before being issued. Hence, they are considerably more expensive.

Any SSL certificate provider is going to offer both kinds, and more. Your decision, however should be mostly based on browser compatibility. Don't go for something $20 less just to find out that it doesn't work with an older version of IE or Safari. You'd be amazed how many people still actually use IE6. The flip side of that is ensure compatibility with newer browsers, such as Google Chrome.

RapidSSL or GeoTrust is usually a good place to start, or your hosting / registrar company may offer them to existing customers at a s
ans:
If you already have an SSL certificate, the main question is whether your hosting provider supports installing and using that certificate on the site. The advice here is that SSL certificates are generally issued for different needs, and any provider should support standard certificates, but compatibility with browsers matters most.

A basic certificate is usually enough for encrypted connections. For e-commerce or anything involving credit card or bank info, a higher-verification certificate is recommended.

Since the site already has a certificate, the closest guidance is to check with the host or registrar whether they allow bringing your own cert and whether it will work across older and newer browsers. RapidSSL or GeoTrust are mentioned as common options if you need a provider.

q: How to Estimate Needed Bandwidth for New Web Application?
ans:
Use the first formula as a starting point:

(Average daily visitors × average page views per visitor × average page size)
+ (average daily file downloads × average file size)
then multiply by 31 and a fudge factor.

The main caveat is that it can be far off if your site uses lots of external images, client-side caching, or AJAX that loads only small amounts of data. Also, “average page views” should mean the average number of pages each visitor views, not total site page views.

So, estimate with that formula, then adjust for how your application actually delivers content.

q: What methods are effective/necessary to quickly remove URLs from the Google index?
ref:
As I see it, you basically have two problems:

Google keeps returning the mistakenly created duplicate URLs in search results, confusing users, and

Googlebot keeps trying to recrawl the duplicate URLs, slowing down the crawling of your actual pages.

The first problem is more serious, since you're actually losing visitors.  The best way to solve it would be to return HTTP 301 permanent redirects from the accidentally created URLs to the correct ones, so that your visitors will be sent to the page they were looking for.  This will also eventually result in search engines dropping the redirected URLs from their index.

(Using 301 instead of 302 redirects here is important, since search engines interpret a 301 redirect as an instruction to index the target URL instead of the source.)

For the second problem, I'd recommend creating (and regularly updating) an XML sitemap of your actual pages.  This will not completely stop Googlebot from crawling the accidentally created URLs (and you don't want it to, since the bot needs to find the 301 redirects), but it will keep the bot informed about updates to your actual pages, so that it can recrawl them faster.

As long as your servers can keep up with the load, you may also want to temporarily increase the maximum crawl rate for your site in Webmaster Tools.
ans:
The effective/necessary method is to return HTTP 301 permanent redirects from the bad URLs to the correct URLs. That tells search engines to drop the old URLs and index the target instead. If the URLs are already fixed and now return 404s, Google will eventually remove them, but that can take time.

To help Google recrawl the right pages faster, keep an XML sitemap of the actual pages updated. You can also temporarily increase the crawl rate in Webmaster Tools if your server can handle it.

The evidence does not support a separate batch-removal tool as the best solution; it suggests redirects as the main fix.

q: Google pulls keywords from only two pages

Search engines work on the assumption of an or search criteria meaning "show any pages that matches "another" or "keyword". Words that match both are just considered more relevant than those that do not. To make this search and and search you either have to use the + operator before each keyword or wrap the search terms in quotes (meaning exactly this phrase).
ans:
This is expected. Adding a second keyword can return more results because Google treats the terms as an OR-style search by default, not as “must match both.” So pages containing either word can appear, and pages matching both are ranked as more relevant.

If you want Google to require both words, use the + operator before each keyword or put the terms in quotes to search for the exact phrase.

q: How to move a single page of content to a new domain
ref:
You seem to have it pretty much nailed.

The important part is having 301 redirects from all the old URLs to the corresponding page on the new site.  If you're keeping your site structure the same and just changing the domain name, it's pretty easy: just set up a general redirection rule (e.g. with Apache mod_rewrite) from oldsite.com/foo/bar?what=ever to newsite.com/foo/bar?what=ever.

As Anagio suggests, it's also a good idea to try and get other sites to update their links so they point directly to the new domain.  However, that's not particularly important — while 301 redirects used to lose a small amount of PageRank, that's no longer the case.  A more important reason for trying to get people to update their links is that you presumably want to build some brand recognition around your new domain, and having a mess of two different kinds of links to your site floating around may interfere with that and confuse users.
ans:
The key is to 301-redirect the old page URL to the corresponding page on the new domain. If you’re moving only one page, make sure that exact old URL goes to the exact new URL, preserving the path and query string if needed. If the site structure stays the same, a general redirect rule can handle it.

Also update any external links you control so they point directly to the new domain. You can notify Google through Webmaster Tools, but the essential part is the 301 redirect.

q: help with htaccess code for navigation
ref:
Try this in your .htaccess file:

Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.olddomain.com$[OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^olddomain.com$
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]

If it's not keeping the query string, try changing the last line of the code above to

RewriteRule / http://www.newdomain.com/?%{QUERY_STRING} [R=301,L]

edit:

If you only want to limit the rule to www.my-website.com/click-4559226-10388358, then try changing the last line of the code above to this:

    RewriteRule ^click\-([0-9]+)\-([0-9]+)$ http://www.newdomain.com/click-$1-$2?%{QUERY_STRING} [R=301,L]
ans:
If you only want URLs like `http://www.my-website.com/click-4559226-10388358`, the closest matching rule is:

`RewriteRule ^click\-([0-9]+)\-([0-9]+)$ http://www.newdomain.com/click-$1-$2?%{QUERY_STRING} [R=301,L]`

That keeps the two numeric parts and passes along the query string.

If you want to redirect the exact path plus everything after it, the broader rule shown is:

`RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]`

The provided example only covers redirecting matching paths on the same pattern; it doesn’t explain handling more complex variations.

ans:

Unless you want to spend time engineering and re-engineering your solution over time to fight spam, I doubt you want to fight this battle... but if you feel compelled to take on the spammers, here is how you might go about it:

Require verified user accounts - This means you will need to collect data from your users and verify that data (whether it be an e-mail address, payment information, or a phone number).

Avoid automated destructive actions - Don't delete anything until a moderator has had a chance to review the merit of user-reported spam. An example: vBulletin comment flagging and moderation.

q: Is there a way to control spam on a site where user contribution is allowed without accounts?
ref:
One alternative to CAPTCHA and less intrusive with better UX is the honeypot method. It's rather simple: you create an input field in the HTML that you hide with javascript. You then check on the server side whether it was filled in or not, if left empty the visitor is human, if filled in a bot.

The reason it works is because javascript is still too computationally expensive for spambots to use (spam is about quantity not quality) so they don't bother parsing it. Originally CSS was suggested to hide the field, however many spambots do parse CSS to detect hidden elements on a page as it's not that expensive.

A friend of mine who told me about the method reported so far a 100% success rate in protecting his sign-up forms using this little neat trick.
ans: Yes. A low-friction option is a honeypot field: add a hidden input to the HTML, hide it with JavaScript, and verify server-side that it remains empty. If it’s filled in, it’s likely a bot. This is especially useful when you want to reduce spam without requiring accounts. It’s not a complete guarantee, but it has strong success on sign-up forms because many spambots skip JavaScript and may not detect the hidden field.

q: new domain, old links are 301'd from old domain to new, how will this affect my rankings?
ref:
From practical experience we've found that beyond the usual 301 redirecting these following actions have resulted in a shorter (and on one occasion non-existent) Search Engine fluctuation:

Time the migration well away from your domain name expiry/renewal, so there is little ambiguity over it being a different site

Set all far-future HTTP expiry headers to the date/time that the website is to be changed, relative timestamps require a little fiddling to become absolute when they are close enough

Migrate slowly, backporting as much as you can so the site runs in parallel - Google has a learning process to "trust" your site - if all paths are suddenly 301's it sometimes backs off indexing only to come back a day or two later, during which time your ranking plumets

Have your new site structure up early (and in parallel) using sitemaps to usher search engines towards the correct URL paths - when it gets to the point that you're now using 301 messages to enforce the change, there'll be additional trust between the Search Engines and yourself

Remember that if you find that there will be duplicate URL paths, use the

Link: <http://www.example.com/my/new/page>; rel="canonical"

HTTP Header to signal your correct destination (there is a META tag version too).

If your linking structure/position is changing drastically the best advice is to ask "is it in the users best interest?"
ans:
Using 301 redirects from the old domain to the new one is the recommended approach, and it helps preserve access to existing links while search engines understand the new URLs.

That said, the guidance provided doesn’t say exactly how rankings will change. It does support updating internal links to the new URLs, updating sitemaps, and using 301s for old URLs. If duplicate paths exist, use canonical links. For the smoothest migration, roll out changes in parallel where possible and avoid doing it near domain renewal/expiry.

So: 301s are the right setup for protecting rankings during a move, but some ranking fluctuation can still happen.

q: Google pulls keywords from only two pages
ref: This is expected behaviour. When you add more keywords to your search you add more possibilities of pages within your site to match any of those keywords. Search engines work on the assumption of an or search criteria meaning "show any pages that matches "another" or "keyword". Words that match both are just considered more relevant than those that do not. To make this search and and search you either have to use the + operator before each keyword or wrap the search terms in quotes (meaning exactly this phrase).
ans:
Google’s default search is like an OR search, not an AND search, so it can return pages matching either term. That means adding a keyword does not always narrow results, and pages matching both terms may rank higher while pages matching just one term can still appear.

If you want Google to require both words, search with + before each term or put the words in quotes for an exact phrase. This is the closest guidance supported by the available information.

q: How would Spanish text at bottom of English content page change how our pages rank?

If the intended audience for (say) http://www.example.com/bangkok/en/ is specifically people in Bangkok then you should probably server two versions of that content, one in the actual regional language and one in English and denote the pages using the appropriate language code. But if your intended audience is English speaking international travellers then it should remain in English and probably not be targeted to any particular country.

.htaccess

q: Bootstrap hidden text and page rank
ref:
Google expects that when a user searches for a phrase and then clicks on your site, the user will be able to find the text that the user searched for.     That means that any text that has keywords in it should be shown to all users without requiring interaction on the page.

In addition to incurring a specific penalty assessed by Google if they detect "hidden text", users tend to back out of your site when they don't find what they are looking for.  Your rankings will fall drastically for any query where users bounce back to Google and look for something else.  Google measures the "return to SERPs" and will de-rank pages that don't do well on this metric for a search term.

That being said, there is no absolute ban on hiding content using CSS or Javascript that the user can then later expose through an action.   Some common examples of this are:

Drop down menus: hidden menu text by default, but exposed on mouse-over

Tool tips: exposed when a user mouses over an element

Tabs: exposed when user clicks on the tab

These techniques are generally fine with Google, regardless of the specific technique used to initially hide the text.    Just be careful not to put keyword rich text into anything that is initially hidden.
ans: Yes. Search engines can evaluate content hidden by CSS or JavaScript, so Bootstrap hidden text may still be seen and potentially affect rankings. That said, normal UI patterns like tabs, dropdowns, and tooltips that reveal content through interaction are generally fine. The main SEO concern is hidden text used to manipulate rankings, especially if important keyword-rich text is hidden on page load and not easily found by users.

q: How to protect a form from spam?
ref:
One alternative to CAPTCHA and less intrusive with better UX is the honeypot method. It's rather simple: you create an input field in the HTML that you hide with javascript. You then check on the server side whether it was filled in or not, if left empty the visitor is human, if filled in a bot.

The reason it works is because javascript is still too computationally expensive for spambots to use (spam is about quantity not quality) so they don't bother parsing it. Originally CSS was suggested to hide the field, however many spambots do parse CSS to detect hidden elements on a page as it's not that expensive.

A friend of mine who told me about the method reported so far a 100% success rate in protecting his sign-up forms using this little neat trick.
ans: A simple way described here is to use a honeypot field: add a hidden form field to the form and check it on the server. If the field is left empty, the submission is likely human; if it’s filled, it’s likely a bot. This can help reduce spam without requiring user accounts and without using CAPTCHA.

q: Preloading web fonts with visibility: hidden; bad for SEO?
ref:
Google expects that when a user searches for a phrase and then clicks on your site, the user will be able to find the text that the user searched for.     That means that any text that has keywords in it should be shown to all users without requiring interaction on the page.

In addition to incurring a specific penalty assessed by Google if they detect "hidden text", users tend to back out of your site when they don't find what they are looking for.  Your rankings will fall drastically for any query where users bounce back to Google and look for something else.  Google measures the "return to SERPs" and will de-rank pages that don't do well on this metric for a search term.

That being said, there is no absolute ban on hiding content using CSS or Javascript that the user can then later expose through an action.   Some common examples of this are:

Drop down menus: hidden menu text by default, but exposed on mouse-over

Tool tips: exposed when a user mouses over an element

Tabs: exposed when user clicks on the tab

These techniques are generally fine with Google, regardless of the specific technique used to initially hide the text.    Just be careful not to put keyword rich text into anything that is initially hidden.
ans:
Yes, text hidden with CSS can still be visible to search engines if it’s in the HTML. So if web-font preloading uses `visibility: hidden`, the content may still be seen by crawlers.

What matters is the purpose. If the hidden text is part of normal UX and is later shown to users through ordinary interaction, that’s generally fine. But if it’s keyword-rich and hidden mainly to influence rankings, it can be treated as hidden text/cloaking and may be risky for SEO.

This answer only supports the general point that CSS-hidden text can still be indexed; it doesn’t specifically confirm any SEO effect of font preloading itself.

q: Why Wikipedia does not have duplicate content issues with search engines?
ref:
The drop in visibility in search is almost certainly unrelated to the parallel website. 

Almost all websites have content hosted on multiple URLs within the same website. That's something which search engines have to deal with. There's no reason to penalize a website for having that & certainly at Google there's no duplicate content penalty when it comes to your own content. 

The effects you'd see (with content duplication within a website) are:

Google's algorithms will choose one URL to show for the content in search. Maybe it won't choose the URL you'd choose. If you have a preference, make it known (through redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, etc). 

Depending on the amount of duplication (is each piece of content hosted 2x, 20x or 200x?), it can happen that the process of crawling is too much for the server, or that new/updated content isn't picked up as quickly as it otherwise might be. 

With a "reasonable" amount of duplication (in your case, just 2x?) and with a reasonably strong server, neither of these are real problems. Most users won't notice the choice of URL, and crawling can still be sufficient.
ans:
Wikipedia likely avoids duplicate-content problems because search engines generally do not punish a site just for having the same content on multiple URLs. If content appears in multiple categories or places, the main effect is usually that one URL may be chosen over another, rather than a penalty.

What matters more is helping search engines understand which version is primary. Using redirects where appropriate, rel=canonical, and clear internal linking can reduce confusion and make crawling and indexing more efficient.

So the closest supported answer is: duplicate content alone usually is not a penalty issue; it mainly affects which URL gets shown and how efficiently search engines index the site.

To reduce risk and rank better, avoid copying large chunks wholesale. Make sure your page includes original content and does not rely on copied text as the main substance.

q: .html extension or no for SEO purposes
ref:

In any case, if when a request for http://www.example.com/answer/my-question-no-1 is interpreted for a server side language, like PHP, ASP, perl, etc that generates certain load, if you change that to http://www.example.com/answer/my-question-no-1.html, you are adding, most probably, a layer of processing to the server since Apache, or whichever web server installed would have to use rewriting rules to parse that information.

If you can skip the web server, not doing any extra rewrite, then the request would go to the same file, index.php for instance, that is doing the processing now, but that file would have to remove the extension, which is not much work, but is unnecessary.

Conclusion, don't do it, there is no benefit at all but could be some drawbacks.

If your pages are generated dynamically, a clean format like /answer/my-question-no-1 is acceptable. In some cases, adding .html can add unnecessary processing or drawbacks if URL rewriting is needed.

ref: Here's my wild stab in the dark: configure your web server to return 304 for every image request, then crowd-source the recovery by posting a list of URLs somewhere and asking on the podcast for all your readers to load each URL and harvest any images that load from their local caches. q: Why Google skips page title
ref:
Google may change the title of your page in their search results (since 2012-01):

We use many signals to decide which title to show to users, primarily the <title> tag if the webmaster specified one. But for some pages, a single title might not be the best one to show for all queries, and so we have algorithms that generate alternative titles to make it easier for our users to recognize relevant pages.

See also the documentation at http://support.google.com/webmasters/bin/answer.py?hl=en&answer=35624:

Google's generation of page titles and descriptions (or "snippets") is completely automated and takes into account both the content of a page as well as references to it that appear on the web. The goal of the snippet and title is to best represent and describe each result and explain how it relates to the user's query.

[…]

While we can't manually change titles or snippets for individual sites, we're always working to make them as relevant as possible.

If they have largely the same content, but not 100% the same content - and you don't want one of the domains disappear from the index, you have to put some effort in it.

Before rel=canonical was introduced by Google, you had two options: Use a robots META tag and specify NOINDEX,FOLLOW on the content that was duplicate or use the content with an iFRAME as this was just a reference.

ans: If the duplicate subdomains or HTTPS/HTTP versions are both accessible and contain the same content, search engines may treat them as duplicate content. The supported approach is to point each duplicate page to the preferred version with rel=canonical, and/or use noindex,follow on the version you do not want indexed. If possible, make one version the only indexable copy or add unique content to the duplicate version. This is about avoiding both copies being indexed; it does not necessarily mean an automatic penalty.

q: What is duplicate content and how can I avoid being penalized for it on my site?
ref:
The drop in visibility in search is almost certainly unrelated to the parallel website. 

Almost all websites have content hosted on multiple URLs within the same website. That's something which search engines have to deal with. There's no reason to penalize a website for having that & certainly at Google there's no duplicate content penalty when it comes to your own content. 

The effects you'd see (with content duplication within a website) are:

Google's algorithms will choose one URL to show for the content in search. Maybe it won't choose the URL you'd choose. If you have a preference, make it known (through redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, etc). 

Depending on the amount of duplication (is each piece of content hosted 2x, 20x or 200x?), it can happen that the process of crawling is too much for the server, or that new/updated content isn't picked up as quickly as it otherwise might be. 

With a "reasonable" amount of duplication (in your case, just 2x?) and with a reasonably strong server, neither of these are real problems. Most users won't notice the choice of URL, and crawling can still be sufficient.
ans:
Duplicate content is the same content appearing on multiple URLs. Based on this, having the same content under multiple categories is unlikely to cause a duplicate-content penalty by itself. Search engines generally do not punish a site just for that.

The main risk is that one URL may be chosen over another, and heavy duplication can make crawling and indexing less efficient. To reduce issues, use redirects where appropriate, rel=canonical, and clear internal linking so search engines know which version is the main one.

ans:

- Make sure the site’s pages are consistently accessible on one preferred URL version.
- Avoid having the same page available under multiple URL versions if possible.

Update the URLs in your sitemap

Use the Fetch as Google tool to trigger crawling your site

q: How to make a Line[] with no end?
Plotting equipotentials gone wrong
ref:
This is just to get an answer on record so the question can be removed from not-answered list.

As rm -rf pointed out in a comment to the question, the difference between E2 and the constant E1 is extremely small, so a plot of E2 is essentially a flat line at 180. If the difference between E2 and E1 is plotted, something useful is obtained.

With[{m = 1, c = 299792458, E1 = 180},
  E2[ϕ_] := E1/(1 + E1 (1 - Cos[ϕ Degree])/(m c^2));
  Plot[E1 - E2[ϕ], {ϕ , 0, 360}, WorkingPrecision -> 20]]
ans:
The plot is disappearing because E2 is extremely close to the constant E1 = 180 for all angles, so the curve is essentially flat and the change is too small to see. With your values, the difference between E2 and E1 is tiny, so Plot may look blank or like a straight line.

A useful fix is to plot the difference instead:

With[{m = 1, c = 299792458, E1 = 180},
  E2[ϕ_] := E1/(1 + E1 (1 - Cos[ϕ Degree])/(m c^2));
  Plot[E1 - E2[ϕ], {ϕ, 0, 360}, WorkingPrecision -> 20]]

That should show the variation more clearly.

q: Square both sides of an equation?
ref:
Try

Expand[(x + y)^2] 

which will give you 

  $ x^2 + 2 x y + y^2$

Even ExpandAll[] won't separate the $"2 xy"$ into $"xy+yx"$. And this makes sense; what should it make of $"3xy"$? $"xy + yx + xy"$, or $"xy + yx +yx"$? And what about $"10 xy"$ (I don't want to think about  $"10000 xy"$)?

J.M.'s solution

Distribute[(x + y) ** (x + y)] /. t_ ** t_ :> t^2  

will give you the $2 x y$ as separate terms, but has to use the symbol for non-commutative multiplication (for example, x and y may be operators):

  $ x^2 + y^2 + x ** y + y** x $

and Mathematica won't interpret it as commutative multiplication. Replacing x and y with numerical values

x^2 + y^2 + x ** y + y ** x /. {x -> 2, y -> 3}

will yield 

  $13 + 2 ** 3 + 3 ** 2$

instead of

  $ 25$
ans:
If you want to square both sides of an equation in Mathematica, `Expand[(x + y)^2]` is the standard way to expand the square. It gives `x^2 + 2 x y + y^2`.

If you specifically want the cross terms split apart, `Expand` won’t do that. A workaround is to use noncommutative multiplication:

`Distribute[(x + y) ** (x + y)] /. t_ ** t_ :> t^2`

This can produce terms like `x ** y` and `y ** x`, but Mathematica will treat them as noncommutative, so it won’t evaluate them like ordinary multiplication.

q: Revolve A Function Around the Y axis?
ref:
This is not a full solution, but here's a start.  It would be useful if you could provide the grayscale and the overlaid coloured components separately because it looks like the grayscale part should control the opacity and the colours need to be added afterwards.

Get the image:

source = Import["https://i.sstatic.net/W76CQ.jpg"];

Reflect because we will rotate around the top edge.  Negate because white in the original needs to be transparent.  

img = ColorNegate@ImageReflect[source, Top -> Bottom]

Aspect ratio:

len = Divide @@ N@ImageDimensions[img]

Interpolating functions, one per channel:

{r, g, b} = ListInterpolation[#, {{0, 1}, {0, len}}] & /@ ImageData /@ ColorSeparate[img];

In a full solution each would be converted to 3D, then combined using ColorCombine.

Rotate to generate 3D data:

step = 0.02;
data = Table[With[{rad = Sqrt[x^2 + y^2]}, If[rad > 1, 0, g[rad, z]]], {x, -1, 1, step}, {y, -1, 1, step}, {z, 0, len, step}]; // AbsoluteTiming

This took about 30 seconds on my machine.  Increase step when experimenting to reduce resolution and let the computation finish faster.

Visualize:

Image3D[data, ClipRange -> {All, {0, 1/step}, {0, 1/step}}, ColorFunction -> "RainbowOpacity"]

This is a single channel image, so I used a colour function that makes it easier to see what's going on.  

Ideally you'd compute this for the grayscale background, which will serve as the opacity channel, then for the red-blue overlay (red and blue channels), then finally ColorCombi
ans:
Yes. The supported approach is to rotate the 2D image data into a 3D volume by sampling points with radius `Sqrt[x^2 + y^2]` and using an interpolating function from the image. A sketch of the method is:

- Import the image
- Reflect it if needed so the rotation axis is along the top edge
- Build interpolating functions for the image channels
- Generate 3D data with `rad = Sqrt[x^2 + y^2]`
- Visualize with `Image3D`

For example, one channel was handled like this:

`data = Table[With[{rad = Sqrt[x^2 + y^2]}, If[rad > 1, 0, g[rad, z]]], {x,-1,1,step}, {y,-1,1,step}, {z,0,len,step}]`

The answer also notes that for a full color result, you’d compute grayscale for opacity and the color channels separately, then combine them.

q: Defining Piecewise Functions
ref:
Let's say you have a list 

data = {5, 1, 3, 8};

and you want to create a Piecewise function creator. First, you need to think about how to construct each of the linear functions. E.g. from x=1 to x=2 we need a linear function going from 5 down to 1. From x=2 to x=3 we need a function going from 1 up to 3 and so on. This is simple math, but you can also use Mathematica for this:

Rescale[x, {pos, pos + 1}, {y1, y2}] // FullSimplify
(* (1 + pos - x) y1 + (-pos + x) y2 *)

This is the expression which interpolates the x-range from pos to pos+1 where y1 is its starting value and y2 the value at the right end. For our piecewise-creator we need to fill this expression for all adjacent pairs

{{5,1},{1,3},{3,8}}

The above structure can easily be created with the help of Partition. The only thing that's left is a function which takes two values and inserts them into our linear function expression. Putting everything together gives our piecewise-function-creator

createPiecewise[l_List] := Piecewise[MapIndexed[
   With[{pos = First[#2], y1 = First[#], y2 = Last[#]},
     {y1 (1 + pos - x) + y2 (x - pos), pos <= x < pos + 1}] &, 
   Partition[l, 2, 1]]
  ]

Testing it with our data and we get

  

Now you can work with it or plot it

Plot[createPiecewise[data], {x, 1, 4}]

q: How do I create inline TraditionalForm expressions, and control their formatting?
ref:
You're not going to get this to work on raw TextData cells. The FE evaluates TextData cells using EnterTextPacket, which merely sends a string along. And, so, the contents must be encoded as a string. Which means you're going to lose all of your typesetting structure. So, let's assume that you've embedded the above cell in a typeset cell where we'll have some more choices.  E.g.,

Cell[BoxData[Cell[TextData[{
  "hello ",
  Cell[BoxData[
   FormBox[
    FractionBox["3", "x"], TraditionalForm]]]
 }]]], "myText",
 Evaluatable->True,
 CellEvaluationFunction->myEvalFun]

Now the FE is going to send an EnterExpressionPacket which maintains the full box structure, including inline cells, and that we can work with. From that starting point, I wrote a version of myEvalFun which works for your sample input. It's not very robust...in particular, it assumes that the cell contains one TextData cell with, at most, one level of BoxData cells inside of it. And that the contents of the TextData cell contain nothing other than strings and BoxData cells (other valid TextData contents include StyleBoxes, ButtonBoxes, and TextData cells). But I think it'll give you a good starting point to work from.

myEvalFun[boxes_, form_] := Module[{inlineExprs, val, topExpr},
  inlineExprs = 
   Cases[boxes, 
    Cell[val : BoxData[_], ___] :> 
     "PP" <> ToString[TeXForm[ToExpression[val, form]]] <> "PP", 
    Infinity];
  topExpr = boxes[[1]] /. Cell[_BoxData, ___] :> "``";
  topExpr = 
   topExpr /. {Ce
ans:
You can’t reliably do this from raw TextData cells, because they’re evaluated as strings and inline typesetting gets stripped. The workable approach is to put the content in a typeset cell so the front end sends box structure instead.

Example shape:

Cell[BoxData[Cell[TextData[{
  "hello ",
  Cell[BoxData[FormBox[FractionBox["3","x"], TraditionalForm]]]
}]]], "myText", Evaluatable->True, CellEvaluationFunction->myEvalFun]

Then your evaluation function can walk the boxes, keep ordinary text unchanged, and replace inline BoxData with whatever wrapper you want, for example:

PP<>ToString[TeXForm[ToExpression[val, form]]]<>PP

The provided solution is limited: it assumes mostly strings plus BoxData, and only one nested level.

q: How to simulate with a user specified bivariate continuous probability distribution
ref:
You need ProbabilityDistribution.

Example:

distr = ProbabilityDistribution[E^(-(x^2/2))/Sqrt[2 π], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]

Mean[distr] (* ==> 0 *)

Variance[distr] (* ==> 1 *)

Warning:

You are responsible for ensuring that the probability density function you provide is normalized over its domain.  Mathematica will not verify this and will not warn you if it isn't, however it will give you incorrect results when using the distribution.  I know from experience that e.g. Variance and RandomVariate will give incorrect results in this case.
ans:
Use ProbabilityDistribution to define the density, then RandomVariate to simulate from it.

For a bivariate continuous distribution, specify both variables and their domain, for example:
d = ProbabilityDistribution[pdf[x, y], {x, xmin, xmax}, {y, ymin, ymax}];

Then:
RandomVariate[d, n]

This supports other distribution commands too, such as Mean and Variance, as long as the pdf is correctly normalized over its domain. If it is not normalized, results from commands like RandomVariate and Variance can be incorrect.

q: Import LaTeX from Wikipedia to Mathematica
ref:
Only expected to work for Mac OS X and linux (Windows has ghostscript, but calls have different syntax):

The reason why the errors happen in the first place is that pdflatex generates one of the more recent versions of the PDF specification (1.5), whereas Mathematica expects an older version upon import (probably 1.3). Specifying the lower version by adding \pdfminorversion=3 as the first line of the source gets rid of the error messages but doesn't fix the spacings.

A possible work-around is to replace the ghostscript call in the question by a two-step process that first converts the $\LaTeX$ generated to Postscript and then passes it to the ps2pdf command which also comes with the $\TeX$ distribution. This seems to remove the features of the modern PDF that trip up Mathematica's import handling:

Run["gs -sDEVICE=pswrite -dNOCACHE -sOutputFile=- -q \
-dbatch -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET words.pdf -c quit | ps2pdf - wordNew.pdf"]

(* ==> 0 *)

Import["wordNew.pdf"]

To tie this together into a Mathematica function that typesets a given source string, I'll change the standard preamble of the test file above into something nicer:

latex[str_] := Module[
  {p,
   TeXsource = "\n\\nonstopmode
    \\documentclass[border=1pt]{standalone}
    \\usepackage[usenames]{color} %used for font color
    \\usepackage{amssymb} %maths
    \\usepackage{amsmath} %maths
    \\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc} %useful to type directly diacritic \
characters\n
    \\begin{document}\n
    ***BODY***
    \\end{doc
ans:
The supported workaround is to typeset the LaTeX externally, then import the generated PDF into Mathematica. On Mac OS X and Linux, a more reliable path is to convert the PDF to PostScript with Ghostscript and then back to PDF with ps2pdf before importing:

Run["gs -sDEVICE=pswrite -dNOCACHE -sOutputFile=- -q -dbatch -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET words.pdf -c quit | ps2pdf - wordNew.pdf"]
Import["wordNew.pdf"]

Direct PDF import is known to be buggy, and using `\pdfminorversion=3` may reduce errors but does not fix spacing issues. The post also mentions a Mathematica function `latex[str_] := Module[...]` to automate this, but the snippet is incomplete here.

q: Graphing the amount of time a function takes
ref:
You can approach these recursive functions in a number of ways (as comments refer to or link to).

Using your arbitrary choice of values for $a,b,c,d$ and variable starting value I illustrate two approaches to motivate playing to achieve desired exploration.

f[a_, b_, c_, d_, x_] := (c - a + d x)/b
rec[s_, n_] := NestList[f[1, 3, 2, -1, #] &, s, n];
fun[a_, b_, c_, d_, u_, 
  s_] := (p[n] /. 
     First@RSolve[p[n + 1] == (c - a + d p[n])/b, p[n], n] /. {C[1] ->
       s}) /. n -> u
Manipulate[Column[{
   ListPlot[rec[st, 10], Filling -> Axis, Frame -> True],
   DiscretePlot[fun[1, 3, 2, -1, u - 1, -st/3], {u, 1, 11, 1}, 
    AxesOrigin -> {0, 0}, Frame -> True]}],
 {{st, 0, "start"}, {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}}]

Some of the code is just to adjust indices so plots would line up.
ans:
You can graph it by defining the recurrence and then generating successive terms. For example, with your values:

p[k_] := (2 - 1 - p[k - 1])/3

Then use NestList or a similar recursive tool to produce the sequence from a starting value, and plot those points.

If you want a closed-form expression instead of step-by-step recursion, the supported approach shown is to solve the recurrence with RSolve, then substitute the starting value. That lets you plot the function over k.

For oscillation, the key is to choose coefficients so the multiplier on p[k-1] causes alternating sign or repeated crossing; in your example, the coefficient is -1/3, which does produce alternating behavior.

MapIndexed[

    , {j, 6}, {i, 4}]

q: Why do I have to put Evaluate[] here
ans:
Because `Set` (`=`) has `HoldFirst`, so the left-hand side is not fully evaluated before assignment.

`a[[1]] = 0` assigns into the list `a`, changing its first element to `0`. It does not assign to `v1`.

`Evaluate[a[[1]]] = 0` forces `a[[1]]` to evaluate first, giving `v1`, so the assignment becomes `v1 = 0`.

So:
- `a[[1]] = 0` → first element of `a` becomes `0`
- `Evaluate[a[[1]]] = 0` → `v1` gets the value `0`

If you want to modify the variable named by the list element, `Evaluate` is needed here.

q: How to extract Solve results as variables
ans:
Yes. Capture the result in a variable, then extract values with replacement rules.

For example:
`sol = Solve[...];`
Then use parts of the solution, such as:
`y[1] /. sol[[1]]`

This takes the first solution rule set returned by `Solve` and substitutes it into `y[1]`. If your system has multiple outputs, you can choose the appropriate one from `sol` and apply `/.` to extract the variable values you need.

q: Interested in knowing what substitutions were made to perform an Integrate[]?
ref:
The main difficulty here is that Integrate does not normally thread over addition. In other words, it does not understand that

$$\int f(x) + g(x) \text{d}x = \int f(x) \text{d}x + \int g(x) \text{d}x.$$

In most cases, it is true, but as integration is a limiting process care must be taken in the order of operations. A case where that is not true does not come to mind at the moment, other than involving infinite series, but it is not out of the question that a simplification in the integrand could obscure the relationship between the LHS and RHS, above.  Mathematica, however, does understand

$$\int a(x) f(y) \text{d}y = a(x) \int f(y) \text{d}y,$$

as shown by

Integrate[a[x] u[y], y]
(*
 a[x] Integrate[u[y], y]
*)

A method to achieve the form you are looking for is to Map Integrate across the sum, Expand[f[x,y]^2], as follows

ints = Integrate[#, y]& /@ Expand[f[x,y]^2]
(*
  a[x]^2*Integrate[u[y]^2, y] + 2*a[x]*b[x]*Integrate[u[y]*v[y], y] 
+ b[x]^2*Integrate[v[y]^2, y]
*)

Then, ReplaceAll (/.) works just fine,

ints /. Integrate[u[y]^2, y] -> I11
(*
  I11*a[x]^2 + 2*a[x]*b[x]*Integrate[u[y]*v[y], y] 
+ b[x]^2*Integrate[v[y]^2, y]
*)
ans:
To get the substitutions to work, first distribute Integrate over the sum by mapping it over each term, since Integrate does not automatically thread across addition. For example:

ints = Integrate[#, y] & /@ Expand[f[x, y]^2]

This produces separate Integrate[...] expressions for each term, such as Integrate[u[y]^2, y]. Then ReplaceAll works:

ints /. Integrate[u[y]^2, y] -> I11

q: Filling a polygon with a pattern of insets
Ordering the Terms in an Expression
ref:
I am not sure of your level of Mathematica experience, or the context of your need.  Some basic facts about Mathematica may be helpful.

Mathematica sorts output lexicographically (roughly alphabetic order). So if you have a choice of variable names make all of the complex coefficients later in the alphabet than the real coefficients. e.g. 

ComplexExpand[a + r I + b + s I + d] 

 a + b + d + I (r + s).

Mathematica assumes that unassigned variables are in general complex numbers. ComplexExpand[] overrides this assumption.  You can also do it manually with something like: Simplify[Re[exp], Assumptions -> {Element[{a, b, c, d, e, f}, Reals]}], which will give the real part of the expression, assuming the listed coefficients are Real.

I hope that you find this helpful.
ans:
Mathematica orders terms lexicographically by default, so one practical approach is to choose variable names so the real-coefficient terms come first and the imaginary coefficients later. For example:

ComplexExpand[a + r I + b + s I + d]

gives

a + b + d + I (r + s)

If you want Mathematica to treat symbols as real, you can also use assumptions, e.g. Simplify[Re[exp], Assumptions -> {Element[{a, b, c, d, e, f}, Reals]}], which returns the real part under those assumptions.

q: The /. syntax in numerical methods
ans:
In Mathematica, `/.` is the replacement operator, read as “replace all.” It applies a rule like `expr /. x -> 3`, meaning “in expr, replace x with 3.”

So in numerical methods code, it’s often used to substitute a test function or symbolic values to verify a finite-difference formula, as in `v = Table[x[i], ...]; CDx[v, h]`.

For differentiation itself, the cited material points to `ListCorrelate` for finite-difference stencils and `NDSolve`FiniteDifferenceDerivative` for derivatives on nonuniform grids.

ans:
Your rule fails because `Dot` is `Flat`, but `CenterDot` is not. `Flat` lets the matcher treat a chain like `k·k·k` as a sequence, so a subexpression `k·k` can be found and replaced inside it.

To fix it, give `CenterDot` the `Flat` attribute:

SetAttributes[CenterDot, Flat]

Then `k·k·k //. k·k -> k` will reduce to `k`.

q: How to make a function that evaluates an expression?
ref:
To understand why ComplexInfinity == ComplexInfinity, let's look at how Mathematica handles infinities.  All of Infinity, -Infinity, ComplexInfinity are just displayed forms of DirectedInfinity:

In[1]:= FullForm /@ {Infinity, -Infinity, ComplexInfinity}
Out[1]= {DirectedInfinity[1], DirectedInfinity[-1], DirectedInfinity[]}

DirectedInfinity[z] represents an infinite quantity in the direction of z on the complex plane.  ComplexInfinity is DirectedInfinity[]; i.e., an infinite quantity with an unknown direction.  The reason it cannot be compared is that the direction is unknown.

If you need to test for ComplexInfinity in particular, you can use

something === ComplexInfinity

=== is a structural test that, unlike ==, does not take any mathematical meaning into account.

Finally, for your purpose, I think NumericalQ (your answer) is a very good solution.
ans:
Use a structural test, not `==`:

`expr === ComplexInfinity`

`==` tries to interpret mathematical equality and won’t reliably test for `ComplexInfinity`. If you want to know whether an expression is numerically defined, `NumericalQ[expr]` is also suggested as a good approach.

q: Gram Schmidt Process for functions
ans:
Your code loops because `For[i = 2, i < 7, i++, ...]` keeps running, but `u` is not set up as a list of functions in a way that matches your indexing, and `Function[x, ...]` is unnecessary here.

A direct translation is:

`inn = Integrate[#1*#2, {x, -Pi, Pi}] &;`
`v = x^Range[0, 5];`
`u = ConstantArray[0, Length@v];`
`u[[1]] = v[[1]];`
`Do[
  u[[i]] = v[[i]] - Total@Table[
      u[[j]]*inn[v[[i]], u[[j]]]/inn[u[[j]], u[[j]]],
      {j, 1, i - 1}],
  {i, 2, Length@v}
]`

This gives an orthogonal basis, not normalized. To normalize, divide each `u[[i]]` by its norm.

If you want, I can also show how to do the same for general function sets, not just polynomials.

q: Use FindRoot solution as number in function
ans:
Yes. The key is to make your function accept a numeric input only, so FindRoot passes actual numbers through it rather than symbolic x.

For example, define the function with a numeric pattern test, like:
Obj[A_?(ArrayQ[#, _, NumericQ] &)] := (A.X - B) // Norm;

Then use FindMinimum or a similar numerical solver on that function. The same idea can be used with FindRoot or NDSolve: wrap the computation in a function that evaluates only for numeric arguments.

If you want the result of FindRoot to be used as a number inside another function, assign it first, then extract the value from the rule, for example x /. FindRoot[...] and use that numeric value in later calculations.

q: Issues with creating functions
ref:
Let's do this:

As R.M suggested in the comments, you should learn the way Mathematica defines functions.

Here's how I've defined your functions:

keygen[keybitlength_] := 
  Module[{kbl, kbl1, pPrime, qPrime, nKey, phiOFn, eKey, dKey},
  kbl = 2^(keybitlength/2);
  kbl1 = 2^(keybitlength/2 - 1);
  pPrime = RandomPrime[{kbl1, kbl}];
  qPrime = RandomPrime[{kbl1, kbl}];
  nKey = pPrime*qPrime;
  phiOFn = (pPrime - 1) (qPrime - 1);
  While[eKey = RandomPrime[{2, phiOFn}]; ! CoprimeQ[eKey, phiOFn]];
  dKey = PowerMod[eKey, -1, phiOFn];
  {{eKey, nKey}, {dKey, nKey}}]

encryption[message_, list : {eKey_, nKey_}] := PowerMod[message, eKey, nKey]

decryption[encmessage_, list : {dKey_, nKey_}] := PowerMod[encmessage, dKey, nKey]

Now it's simple to use this for numeric values:

keys = keygen[32]

(*{{1680015751, 2207995403}, {383738359, 2207995403}}*)

encryption[123456, keys[[1]]]

(*1731973844*)

decryption[1731973844,keys[[2]]]

(*123456*)

The best way I can figure out to do strings is a ToCharacterCode method.

Let's redefine the encryption and decryption functions to handle these.

encryption[message_, list : {eKey_, nKey_}] := 
  Module[{temp}, 
  If[StringQ[message], (temp = ToCharacterCode[message];PowerMod[#, eKey, nKey] & /@temp), 
  PowerMod[message, eKey, nKey]]]

decryption[encmessage_, list : {dKey_, nKey_}] := Module[{temp},
  If[ListQ[encmessage], (temp = PowerMod[#, dKey, nKey] & /@ encmessage; 
  FromCharacterCode[temp]), PowerMod[encmessage, dKey, nKey]]]

Test
ans:
The issue is mostly how Mathematica defines and runs functions. Use `:=` with patterns like `keygen[keybitlength_] := ...`, and put local variables inside `Module[{...}, ...]`. Also, if you want a function to take a key pair, define it with a pattern such as `list : {eKey_, nKey_}`.

With those changes, the code can be called explicitly, for example:
`keys = keygen[32]`
`encryption[123456, keys[[1]]]`
`decryption[enc, keys[[2]]]`

For strings, the supported approach in the answer is to convert with `ToCharacterCode` and back with `FromCharacterCode`. The answer does not explain your exact document setup, but it does show the correct function structure and usage.

q: Assumption for all the notebook
ref:
All the demonstrations uploaded to the Wolfram Demonstrations Project (WDP) are CDF documents, which you can open with the CDF player or Player Pro or Mathematica. The CDF player (which is what you open it in, by default) has a set of restrictions. Specifically, you cannot

Create new documents/files or save files

Change or save the state of the kernel/front end

Evaluate or edit input cells

So the possibility of anything being done to your system with a CDF player is minimal. If you're using Mathematica, the program is free to do all of the above (standard warnings for dynamic content still apply).

In addition, Daniel Lichtblau confirms that there is a blacklist of disallowed functions for all submissions that end up on the WDP. These include things that can change the state of your Mathematica session or mess with your OS.

To summarize, I believe it should be safe for you to interact with the demonstration in your browser before downloading.
ans: If you open the demonstrations in the CDF Player, they’re restricted: they can’t create/save files, change or save kernel/front end state, or evaluate/edit input cells. That makes system impact minimal. If you open them in Mathematica itself, they can do those things, so standard caution with dynamic content applies. Also, submissions to the Wolfram Demonstrations Project are filtered by a blacklist of disallowed functions that block things that could alter your Mathematica session or mess with the OS.

q: How to define the tangent gradient operator?

A general idea as to how this can be done in a consistent way is explained in the help documents under NonCommutativeMultiply. The thing is that you want to use your operators in an algebraic notation, and that's what that page discusses. 

If, on the other hand, you're happy with a more formal Mathematica notation, then you would have the easier task of defining operators simply as 

dx := D[#, x] &
dy := D[#, y] &

and using them as follows:

dx@f[x, y, z]

  $f^{(1,0,0)}(x,y,z)$

Combining operators would then be done using Composition: 

dxy = Composition[dx, dy];
dxy[f[x, y, z]]

  $f^{(1,1,0)}(x,y,z)$

Edit

Here is another approach that's sort of intermediate between the very simple D[#,x]& scheme and the more complicated realization of an operator algebra in the linked reference from the documentation.

To make the operators satisfy the axioms of a vector space, we'd have to define their addition among each other and the multiplication with scalars. This can be done most conveniently if we don't use patterns to represent the operators, but Functions. So here I repeat the operator definitions - they act the same way as the dx, dy defined above, but their definition is stored differently:

dx = Function[{f}, D[f, x]];
dy = Function[{f}, D[f, y]];

Now I define the multiplication of an operator with a scalar: 

multiplyOp[scalar_, op_] := Function[{f1}, scalar op[f1]];

For simplicity, I always assume that the scalar is given as the first argument, and the second argumen
ans:
If you mean a derivative-like operator in Mathematica, the simplest definition is:

dx := D[#, x] &
dy := D[#, y] &

Then use them as operators:

dx @ f[x, y, z]

To combine them, use Composition:

dxy = Composition[dx, dy];
dxy[f[x, y, z]]

If you want operators that can be added and scaled more like a vector space, define them as Function objects:

dx = Function[{f}, D[f, x]];
dy = Function[{f}, D[f, y]];

DynamicModule[{trigger = 0},

  EventHandler[Framed["Benjamin Button"], "MouseDown" :> (++trigger)],

q: how to round result to 64 bit double precision number?
ref:
(Based on the comments)

Matrices are best stored by Mathematica in packed arrayes. Packed arrays are limited to certain types. According to the docs‌​: "Supported types are Integer, Real, and Complex. "

Any change to SetPrecision practically applies a tenfold increase in bytes, because SetPrecision[..., small] will cause machine numbers, which might live in a packed array, to become low precision, unpackable, bignums. Big loss in terms of memory due to the unpacking.

Just for the record, IEEE 754-2008 does allow 16-bit floats (Half-precision floating-point format) so it is possible to lower bitwidth in e.g. C, however do take into account the possibility that with lower precision, accumulated error might be much higher in some computations.
ans:
If you mean in Mathematica, you generally can’t “round” a machine-real result down to a smaller floating-point storage type and keep it in a packed array. Machine numbers are already 64-bit doubles, and changing precision with SetPrecision tends to unpack them into larger, slower arbitrary-precision numbers.

So the closest supported answer is: results are already rounded to 64-bit double precision as machine reals. Mathematica does not offer a built-in lower-bitwidth packed float type like half precision in this context.

If you need smaller bitwidths, that would have to be done outside Mathematica or with another system/language that supports 16-bit floats.

q: How to find the local maximum of a list
ref:
While using Ordering as in Mr.Wizard's answer will most likely be the fastest non-compiled solution, it will not return all possible arguments that maximize the return value. Here's a simple way of writing a function that does this:

listMaxArg[f_, list_] := With[{max = f /@ list // Max}, Select[list, f@# == max &]]

Here's an example that compares the two solutions:

a = {{1, 2, 3}, {10}, {6, 4}};
listMaxArg[Total, a] 
(* Out[1]= {{10}, {6, 4}} *)

listMaxArgMrWiz[Total, a]
(*Out[2]= {{6, 4}} *)
ans:
Compute the function on each element, find the maximum, then select the elements whose function value equals that maximum:

listMaxArg[f_, list_] := With[{max = Max[f /@ list]}, Select[list, f[#] == max &]]

For your example:

listMaxArg[Total, {{1, 2, 3}, {10}}]

This returns { {10} }.

If you want only one maximizing element, another approach is to use Ordering, but that may not return all ties.

q: Correspondence between eigenvectors and eigenvalues
ref:
From J.M's comment:

  Usually in the sparse matrix case, one only wants the biggest few or
  smallest few, and only very rarely the entire spectrum. If you're
  asking for a full eigendecomposition, then the effort needed for a
  sparse array should not be too different from the effort needed for a
  dense array.

I checked the timing for a few dense and sparse arrays, both with few and with many non-zero elements.

n = 50;
s = SparseArray[
     Append[
      Thread[
       RandomInteger[{1, 144}, {n, 2}] -> RandomInteger[{1, 20}, n]
      ], {i_, i_} -> 1], 
      {144, 144}
     ]

All eigenvalues:

Do[Quiet[Eigenvalues[s]], {1}]; // AbsoluteTiming
t = s // Normal;
Do[Eigenvalues[t], {1}]; // AbsoluteTiming

Only 2 eigenvalues

Do[Quiet[Eigenvalues[s, 2]], {1}]; // AbsoluteTiming
t = s // Normal;
Do[Eigenvalues[t, 2], {1}]; // AbsoluteTiming

So, not much difference between sparse and dense matrices. Having only a few eigenvalues calculated saves a bit of time but only if the matrix contains many non-zero elements.
ans:
For a full eigendecomposition, sparse and dense methods are usually not very different in effort. Sparse matrices are typically advantageous when you only need a few eigenvalues/eigenvectors, especially the largest or smallest few. If you ask for all eigenvalues/eigenvectors, the sparse input may even be converted to dense because dense methods can be faster.

So the correspondence is:
- full spectrum: sparse is not necessarily faster than dense
- only a few eigenvalues/eigenvectors: sparse can help a bit, mainly for matrices with many nonzero entries

If you want, I can also explain the distinction between “eigenvalues correspond to eigenvectors” and “how many are computed” in this context.

q: Using Thread or MapThread over multi-level, ragged lists
ref:
The simple answer: Thread does not have the attribute HoldAll, so its contents are executed before it processes them.

But, it is not quite that simple. If you add HoldAll, you still don't get what you want

Internal`InheritedBlock[{Thread},
 SetAttributes[Thread, HoldAll];
 Thread[appendTo[list1, list2]]
]
(* {{{1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}, {"a", "b"}}, {{1, 3, 5}, {9, 8}, {"a", "b"}}} *)

which implies that in this form only the first list is threaded over.

Note, I used Internal`InheritedBlock to retain the behavior of Thread while not allowing my modifications to leak.
ans:
`Thread` evaluates its argument before threading, so `appendTo[list1, list2]` runs first and `Map[Append[#, item] &, ll]` is applied with `item = list2`, not elementwise with each `"a"`/`"b"`.

Even if you make `Thread` hold its argument, this still won’t give the desired nesting behavior: it only threads the first list in that form. The result is a pair of lists where the second list is appended as a whole to each top-level element.

`MapThread` is the right tool here, since it maps a function over corresponding elements of multiple lists at the same level.

q: How to graph the revolution of solid limited by 2 points in x axis
ref:
One way to get at the answers you seek is to first define your function:

y[x_] := 1/2 Exp[x] + 1/12 Exp[-3 x]

and then perform the desired operations on that function.  For instance, the volume:

Integrate[Pi y[x]^2, x]

or if you want it evaluated over the region from 0 to 1:

Integrate[Pi y[x]^2,{x,0,1}] //N
(* 2.62579 *)

And the surface area can be obtained from:

2 Pi NIntegrate[y[x] Sqrt[1 + y'[x]^2], {x, 0, 1}]
(* 7.44677 *)

I use NIntegrate in this last example since your function cannot be readily integrated symbolically.
ans:
To graph the solid of revolution between two x-values, first define the curve y[x], then think of the interval {x, a, b} as the part being rotated around the x-axis.

For example, with x from 0 to 1:
y[x_] := 1/2 Exp[x] + 1/12 Exp[-3 x]

You can graph the curve itself with Plot[y[x], {x, 0, 1}], and the volume is found from
Integrate[Pi y[x]^2, {x, 0, 1}]

If you want the curved surface area, use
2 Pi NIntegrate[y[x] Sqrt[1 + y'[x]^2], {x, 0, 1}]

If by “graph the revolution” you mean draw the 3D solid, this answer only covers the setup for the interval and the formulas, not the actual 3D plotting command.
