ref:
There is a literature on denesting radicals. Not really my strength. In cases where you know (or suspect) the specific radicals that should appear in the result you can use a Groebner basis computation to recast your algebraic value via a minimal polynomial. Then factor over the extension defined by those radicals, solve, and pick the solution that is numerically correct (the others being algebraic conjugates). I illustrate with that first example.

rootpoly = 
 GroebnerBasis[{x*xrecip - 1, xrecip - (1 + y - z), y^2 - 2, z^2 - 3},
    x, {xrecip, y, z}][[1]]

(* -1 + 4*x + 4*x^2 - 16*x^3 + 8*x^4 *)

fax = 
 Select[FactorList[rootpoly, Extension -> {Sqrt[2], Sqrt[3]}][[All, 
    1]], ! FreeQ[#, x] &]

(* {2 + Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6] - 4*x, -2 - Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6] + 4*x, 
   2 - Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6] - 4*x, -2 + Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6] + 4*x} *)

candidates = Flatten[Map[x /. Solve[# == 0, x] &, fax]];
First[Select[candidates, (N[#] == 1/(1 + Sqrt[2] - Sqrt[3])) &]]

(* (1/4)*(2 + Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6]) *)

If you are more familiar with manipulating algebraic numbers than you are with Groebner bases, here is a better way to get that defining polynomial.

RootReduce[1/(1 + Sqrt[2] - Sqrt[3])][[1]][x]

(* Out[35]= -1 + 4 x + 4 x^2 - 16 x^3 + 8 x^4 *)

--- edit ---

I will show this in a way that is more automated, in terms of deciding what to use in the extension for factoring. The idea is to allow roots of all factors of all integers that appear in the nested radical.

val = Sqrt[4 + Sqrt[15]];
root
ans:
A practical way is to find the defining polynomial of the expression, factor it over the extension generated by the radicals you expect, and then choose the root that matches the numerical value.

For example, for 1/(1 + Sqrt[2] - Sqrt[3]), you can use RootReduce[1/(1 + Sqrt[2] - Sqrt[3])][[1]][x], which gives

-1 + 4 x + 4 x^2 - 16 x^3 + 8 x^4

Then factor over Extension -> {Sqrt[2], Sqrt[3]}, solve the linear factors, and pick the numerically correct one. This yields (1/4)(2 + Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[6]).

This method also works for similar examples, but it does require guessing which radicals belong in the extension.

q: How to make a control array of buttons or togglers?
How to plot multiple horizontal lines?
ans:
The closest supported approach is to rotate and reflect the plot you want to become horizontal, then overlay it.

For example:

trF = GeometricTransformation[#,
  Composition[ReflectionTransform[{-1, 0}], RotationTransform[Pi/2]]] &;

Then combine:

Show[s1, Graphics@(trF @@ s2)]

or:

Show[s1, MapAt[trF, s2, {1}]]

This is useful when you want multiple curves to share the same horizontal axis by reorienting one set before plotting together.

q: How to set up the font size permanently (i.e. for all notebooks, all future sessions?)
ref:
Stylesheets (as "bill s" said) seem the best idea to me. Just modify the font of the type of cells(Title, section, subsection...) you want on the stylesheet (using the writing assistant palette, for instance) and the changes will be applied to the same cell types on the notebook.

Edit1:

Here are more detailed steps (tested in mathematica 9 front-end):

Go to "Format"-> "Edit Stylesheet"

This opens the "Private style definitions" stylesheet, whose definitions override the base stylesheet  all notebooks have by default. 

From the "Choose style" drop-down menu select the style you want to modify.

A new cell will be created with the contents: "Local definition for style "stylename"" and below: "stylename" formatted according to that particular style.

With the "Writing Assistant" palette change the desired feature (text size, color, font...)

Note that only the features you set will be overriden, all the other will be inherited from the base stylesheet.

You can also modify the cell expression directly if you know how (Ctrl+Shift+e to toggle it on the current cell)

Also, note that the cells in the stylesheet are not regular cells, thus you can't just insert a regular cell in it, use the dropdown "Choose style" instead.

This is what the expression of a stylesheet cell for "Title" looks like (you can toggle between displaying a cell in normal mode and expression mode with Ctrl+Shift+e ): Cell[StyleData["Title"]]. If we changed the color to blue, it would look like this: Cell
ans:
To make the font size permanent for all notebooks and future sessions, edit the notebook stylesheet rather than individual cells.

Go to Format → Edit Stylesheet, then modify the relevant cell styles you use, such as Title, Section, and Text. Set the font size there, either with the Writing Assistant palette or by editing the style definition directly.

If you want the same font size for all text types, update each relevant style in the stylesheet. Only the properties you set will override the base style.

q: How to set up the font size permanently (i.e. for all notebooks, all future sessions?)
ans:
There isn’t a supported single setting shown here for making font size permanent for all notebooks and all future sessions.

The closest supported approach is to use one stylesheet for all notebooks, or set a notebook’s StyleDefinitions before export. The example described loops over all open notebooks, temporarily changes each notebook’s stylesheet or style definitions, exports to PDF, then restores the original stylesheet.

So, based on this, consistent font size is controlled via the notebook stylesheet/style definitions, not by a global permanent font-size switch.

q: How do I get all possible solutions in an underdetermined system?
ref:
eqns = {(300 (1920 + 8 x - 21 y) (-80 + y))/(7 (30 + x)^3) + (2025 (208 x + 
           5 (-3446 + y)))/(52 (90 + y)^2) + (300 (4500 + 80 x - 21 z) (-100 +
            z))/(7 (30 + x)^3) - (1521 (15425 - 539 x + 
           50 z))/(539 (39 + z)^2) == 
     0, -((300 (1920 + 8 x - 21 y))/(7 (30 + x)^2)) - (2025 (-85 + 
           x) (208 x + 5 (-3446 + y)))/(52 (90 + y)^3) + (2025 (49410 + 
           445 y - 208 z) (-45 + z))/(52 (90 + y)^3) - (1521 (19680 - 539 y + 
           90 z))/(539 (39 + z)^2) == 
     0, -((2025 (49410 + 445 y - 208 z))/(52 (90 + y)^2)) - (300 (4500 + 
           80 x - 21 z))/(7 (30 + x)^2) - (1521 (-25 + x) (539 x - 
           25 (617 + 2 z)))/(539 (39 + z)^3) - (1521 (-30 + y) (539 y - 
           30 (656 + 3 z)))/(539 (39 + z)^3) == 0} // Simplify;

vars = Variables[Level[eqns, {-1}]];

allSolns = Solve[eqns, vars] // Simplify;

Length[allSolns]

  47

Since the exact results contain Root objects they are neither explicitly Real nor explicitly Complex.

ro = {z /. allSolns[[47]]};

{Cases[ro, _Real], Cases[ro, _Complex]}

  {{}, {}}

The root objects need to be converted to numbers to be explicitly Complex or Real. Machine precision calculations are too inaccurate when converting the root objects. Specifying a precision will require Mathematica to maintain sufficient precision in the calculations.

realSolns = Cases[allSolns,
   _?(FreeQ[N[#, 16], Complex] &)];

Length[realSolns]

  7

realSolns // N[#, 16] & // Grid[#, Alignment -> Left] &
ans:
If you want all solutions, first generate the full solution set, then filter out any complex ones using a higher-precision numeric check. For example:

realSolns = Cases[allSolns, _?(FreeQ[N[#, 16], Complex] &)];

This keeps all real solutions; in the example it returns 7 real solutions. If the system is underdetermined and you need a single solution, you can then select one element, such as:

N[realSolns[[1]], 16]

If you need a particular solution, you’ll need an ordering or selection criterion, since the set may contain multiple valid roots.

q: Partitioning a list of 2D points into sublists that fit into non-overlapping equal-sized squares
ref:
This is a straightforward application of FindClusters:

ListPlot@FindClusters[#, 2] & /@ Transpose@PairSet // GraphicsRow

See the DistanceFunction and Method options to further fine tune your clustering or use a different metric.
ans:
A simple approach is to cluster the 2D points. For example, you can partition them into subsets with:

ListPlot@FindClusters[#, 2] & /@ Transpose@PairSet // GraphicsRow

This splits the coordinates into two groups. If you need the groups to align more closely with square tiles and avoid overlap, you can tune DistanceFunction and Method, or use a different metric. The provided answer doesn’t fully cover enforcing exact equal-sized squares, but clustering is the closest supported guidance here.

q: Combined NonlinearModelFit
ans:
Use one combined fit, not separate fits. Build a single model that returns all dependent variables, tag each data point with which dataset it belongs to, and fit everything simultaneously. The supported pattern is:

- solve the ODE system parametrically with ParametricNDSolveValue
- combine all observations into one table with a dataset index
- map that index to the matching solution component in the model
- run FindFit or NonlinearModelFit on the combined data

This lets the parameters be determined self-consistently across all datasets. If you want, I can help translate this into a Mathematica template for your specific 3 datasets and 4-equation system.

q: How to restrict global variables to within a given notebook?
ref:
General considerations

It often does make sense to use global variables inside your package. And sometimes, you simply can't avoid that. By global here I mean variables which are defined outside any function. There are two distinct cases here:

A variable is defined in the Private` subsection of the package and not exported as a part of the package's public interface (then it is an "internal" global variable used by the implementation of the package). 

A variable is exported to the user, as a part of the public interface of the package.

In all cases, global variables are useful when the package needs to store some state. There are several cases when this may be needed. I will divide them into two broad categories / sets of use cases:

Certain data must be recorded during the installation (loading) of the package, so that they can be used later. They may or may not need to change later, but it may be that they can only be obtained during the load-time. Some examples of such are various paths to certain resources.  

Some parameters have to be present to store the current state of the package, and are related to the run-time behavior of the package. Such variables may, for example, store the information about which resources / functions have been installed or uninstalled, or some other status variables.

While I agree that one is better off by not using global variables unless strictly necessary, I doubt that one can do without global variables in packages for all tasks. The
ans: There isn’t a single built-in command described here to “localize all variables in a notebook.” The closest supported approach is to use Module or Block to scope variables in the notebook code so they don’t act as global names. If you’re working in a package-style setup, keep internal globals in a Private` context so they stay out of the public interface.

q: Using Through to evaluate complex expressions
ref:
I think you have to do the same as in many such cases: protect your arguments to be strictly numerical:

f[a_?NumericQ, b_?NumericQ] := Abs[(a + I b)^(3/2)];

And  then no problems:

NMinimize[f[a,b],{a,b}]

(*
 ==>  {1.11868*10^-26,{a->3.9489*10^-18,b->3.07007*10^-18}}
*)

Edit:

The following function automatically packs the expression into a function with _?NumericQ pattern arguments:

NOptimize[optfunc_,expr_,vars_,options___]:=
  Module[{f,
          varlist=If[ListQ[vars],vars,{vars}],
          expression=If[ListQ[expr],First@expr,expr],
          conditions=If[ListQ[expr],Rest@expr,{}]},
    Evaluate[f@@(Pattern[#,_?NumericQ]&/@varlist)]=expression;
    optfunc[{f@@varlist}~Join~conditions,vars,options]]

It can be used as follows:

NOptimize[NMinimize, a^2, a, AccuracyGoal->0.01]
(*
--> {2.39829*10^-33,{a->4.89724*10^-17}}
*)

or with constraints:

NOptimize[NMinimize, {a^2, a>3}, a, AccuracyGoal->0.01]
(*
--> {9.,{a->3.}}
*)

The following shows that it indeed solves the problem with LessEqual::Nord:

NOptimize[NMinimize,Abs[(a+I b)^(3/2)],{a,b}]
(*
--> {9.06219*10^-27,{a->4.31982*10^-18,b->4.8223*10^-19}}
*)
ans:
To avoid invalid comparison errors with `Through` or other interpolated expressions, make sure the expression is evaluated only for numeric inputs. The supported pattern is to define the function with `NumericQ` constraints on its arguments, for example:

`f[a_?NumericQ, b_?NumericQ] := Abs[(a + I b)^(3/2)];`

Then use it inside `NMinimize` or similar numeric routines. This prevents symbolic evaluation of complex intermediate expressions that can trigger `LessEqual::nord`-type errors.

The evidence also mentions a helper wrapper, `NOptimize`, which packages an expression into a numeric-only function and works with `NMinimize`, including constraints.

q: Excluding an interval of parameters from Integrate
ref: Assumptions need to be quantified equations or inequalities, so replace your rules with equations.  I'm guessing Integrate probably won't do too much with these, either, so attempt to use FullSimplify on the results with your new assumptions.
ans:
If you want an assumption to exclude part of a parameter range, express it as an inequality, not a replacement rule. For example, use something like x > 0 in Assumptions rather than x -> 0. The supported workflow is often to compute the integral first, then apply FullSimplify with the assumptions, since Integrate may not use them much directly.

If the issue is excluding an interval, the closest supported guidance is to encode that exclusion as inequalities in the assumptions. If simplification still fails, the assumptions may not be in a form the simplifier can use.

q: Why aren't these additions of integrals and summations equal?
ref:
The main difficulty here is that Integrate does not normally thread over addition. In other words, it does not understand that

$$\int f(x) + g(x) \text{d}x = \int f(x) \text{d}x + \int g(x) \text{d}x.$$

In most cases, it is true, but as integration is a limiting process care must be taken in the order of operations. A case where that is not true does not come to mind at the moment, other than involving infinite series, but it is not out of the question that a simplification in the integrand could obscure the relationship between the LHS and RHS, above.  Mathematica, however, does understand

$$\int a(x) f(y) \text{d}y = a(x) \int f(y) \text{d}y,$$

as shown by

Integrate[a[x] u[y], y]
(*
 a[x] Integrate[u[y], y]
*)

A method to achieve the form you are looking for is to Map Integrate across the sum, Expand[f[x,y]^2], as follows

ints = Integrate[#, y]& /@ Expand[f[x,y]^2]
(*
  a[x]^2*Integrate[u[y]^2, y] + 2*a[x]*b[x]*Integrate[u[y]*v[y], y] 
+ b[x]^2*Integrate[v[y]^2, y]
*)

Then, ReplaceAll (/.) works just fine,

ints /. Integrate[u[y]^2, y] -> I11
(*
  I11*a[x]^2 + 2*a[x]*b[x]*Integrate[u[y]*v[y], y] 
+ b[x]^2*Integrate[v[y]^2, y]
*)
ans:
Because `Integrate` and summations don’t necessarily distribute in the way you’re expecting unless the expression is split first. The supported approach is to expand the sum/product, apply `Integrate` term by term, and then perform replacements on each resulting integral.

For example, instead of trying to match a rule on the whole combined integral, do something like:
`Integrate[#, y] & /@ Expand[expr]`

Then apply your substitution rules to the list of individual integrals.

So the closest guidance is: separate the terms first, then integrate and substitute on each term individually.

q: Plot3D has a break in the center of the plot
ref:
As you already know from the comments, increasing MaxRecursion or PlotPoints helps, where I would prefer the first one.

In the case of your function, you can gain some speed by compiling the expression. Then, you can set MaxRecursion to a higher value and the plot is still reasonable fast. The code below runs in about 3 seconds here

m = 60;
With[{cf = (Compile[{{x, _Real, 0}, {y, _Real, 0}},
        #, RuntimeOptions -> "Speed", CompilationTarget -> "C"] & /@

           Flatten[{Re[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]], 
        Im[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]]}])},
  (#1[args__?NumericQ] := #2[args]) & @@@ Transpose[{{f1, f2}, cf}]
  ];

ContourPlot[{f1[x, y], f2[x, y]}, {x, -5, 6}, {y, -10, 10}, 
 AspectRatio -> Automatic, MaxRecursion -> 3]
ans:
The breaks are usually caused by insufficient sampling. The best first thing to try is increasing MaxRecursion. PlotPoints can also help, but MaxRecursion is the better first choice.

If runtime becomes an issue, compiling the expressions can keep higher recursion levels fast. The example guidance was to compile the real and imaginary parts into functions and then use a plot like:

ContourPlot[{f1[x, y], f2[x, y]}, {x, -5, 6}, {y, -10, 10},
 AspectRatio -> Automatic, MaxRecursion -> 3]

This should reduce the broken-looking sections.

q: Is there an analogue of the Variables command for general expressions?
ref:
Perhaps replacing with dummies for simplification?

doThat[expr_, vars_List] := 
 Expand[Simplify[
    expr /. Flatten[
      Solve[# == ToString@#, First@Variables@#] & /@ vars]], 
   Alternatives @@ ToString /@ vars] /. 
  Thread[ToString /@ vars -> vars]

So

doThat[c a (x1 + x2) + d a (x1 + x2) + a (y1 + y2), {x1 + x2, 
  y1 + y2}]

gives

  a (c + d) (x1 + x2) + a (y1 + y2)
ans:
Not as a general built-in analogue. The supported approach here is to work around it by replacing the symbolic subexpressions you want treated as variables with temporary dummies, simplifying, and then substituting them back.

So for general expressions, you can use a helper like the shown `doThat[...]` pattern to specify which subexpressions should behave like variables while leaving constants unchanged.

q: Finding equation of tangent line at a point
ref:
Certainly, there is a better way:

y[x_] := 2 x Sin[x]; a = Pi/2;
Collect[Normal[Series[y[x], {x, a, 1}]], x, Simplify]

Recall that the formula for a Taylor polynomial looks a bit like this:

$$f(x)=\color{red}{f(a)+f^\prime (a)(x-a)}+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(a)}{2}(x-a)^2+\cdots$$

and reconciling this with the geometric interpretation of the Taylor polynomial as the best one-point osculatory (agrees at function and derivative values) approximation of a function shows why the approach works. I believe this should be a standard way to look at Taylor polynomials in the textbooks, if it already isn't.

Here is an equivalent approach:

Collect[InterpolatingPolynomial[{{{a}, y[a], y'[a]}}, x], x, Simplify]

This is based on the fact that the tangent line is the unique Hermite interpolating polynomial of degree $1$.

Certainly, one could do the plodding, "traditional" (whatever that means) approach:

y[x_] := 2 x Sin[x]; a = Pi/2;
Collect[y[a] + y'[a] (x - a), x, Simplify]

In any event, Solve[] is definitely unnecessary here.
ans:
Use the tangent-line formula at the point \(a\):

\(f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)\)

So for a curve `y[x_]`, define the point `a` and compute:

`y[a] + y'[a] (x - a)`

Example:

`y[x_] := 2 x Sin[x];`
`a = Pi/2;`
`Collect[y[a] + y'[a] (x - a), x, Simplify]`

If you want the same result via a first-order Taylor expansion:

`Collect[Normal[Series[y[x], {x, a, 1}]], x, Simplify]`

Both give the tangent line at the chosen point.

q: Sort lists according to the order of another
ref:
There might be a more generalized version of this question here, but I can't find it. In your specific example, I would've probably written it as 

f = Composition[Apply[{First@#, Total@#2} &, #] &, Transpose] /@ GatherBy[Join[##], First]&;

Then you can pass your lists (any number) to it:

f[list1, list2] // Sort
(* {{0, 0.5}, {0.4, 1}, {1, 3}, {1.5, 3}, {2, 4}, {3, 9}, {3.25, 8}, {4, 24}} *)

If you always want a sorted output, you can add it to the definition.

Since you say that you want to add two histograms, there are a couple of alternatives to doing the above (assuming you have control over the data set and the histogram generation)

Combine the data sets and then generate a histogram list for the combined set.

Use explicit bins and generate histogram lists for both sets using the same binning. Adding those two would be much simpler.
ans:
If your lists are already sorted by the first element, you can merge items with the same first entry and add the corresponding second entries. The previous solution groups equal first elements, keeps that first value, and sums the second values in each group.

If you want the result always sorted, add Sort to the function.

For the example given, the sorted output is:
{{0, 0.5}, {0.4, 1}, {1, 3}, {1.5, 3}, {2, 4}, {3, 9}, {3.25, 8}, {4, 24}}

q: Manipulate using a variable defined outside of the manipulate function
ans:
Use the external variable directly inside Manipulate; it does not need to be defined inside the Manipulate body as long as it’s in scope when the cell evaluates.

If the variable contains a symbol, the main issue is usually that the plotted expression should treat that symbol consistently as a parameter, not something to be numerically evaluated. The supported guidance here is only that Manipulate should wrap the plotting function, and any symbolic parameter should be handled consistently.

If you share the actual expression or code, I can help adapt it.

q: Plot showing discontinuity where it shouldn't
ref:
Mathematica even leaves a gap when the expressions in Piecewise are equal, as long as Mathematica doesn't see the equality. Very simple example

test[x_] := Piecewise[{{x, x >= 1}, {Sqrt[x^2], x < 1}}]
Plot[test[x], {x, 0, 2}, PlotStyle -> Thick]

  

When you replace Sqrt[x^2] by x, no gap.

What you have to understand is that the cracks are features when you use Piecewise because usually a piecewise function has jumps or discontinuities. Mathematica really just splits the plot, when it sees Piecewise and cannot determine a simple equality between the expressions.

This is a bit unfortunate, because although it is correct most of the time, users will always complain why this doesn't work like they want it.

My short answer: If you don't want cracks, then use Exclusions->None or make sure Mathematica doesn't see your Piecewise

f[x_?NumericQ] := Piecewise[{{3 x^2 - 3 x + 1, x >= 1}, {x^3, x < 1}}]
Plot[f[x], {x, 0, 1.5}]

Here, the NumericQ hinders Mathematica to evaluate your expression for non-numeric values and the only chance it has is to put a number in and get a number out :-)

Btw, let's give Mathematica something to think about and add a second definition for f where it sees the Piecewise. It doesn't matter what it sees, so screw it:

f[x_] := Piecewise[{{"Ding", x < .4}, {"Dong", x < .8}, {"Boing", x < 1.2}}, "Blub"];

The important part is that Mathematica uses the above definition to see a Piecewise and the gaps it introduces. For plotting, Mathematica has to suppl
ans:
This sounds like a plotting artifact rather than a true discontinuity. Plot can split a Piecewise curve at branch boundaries unless it can prove the pieces match exactly, even if the values and derivatives do.

The fixes supported here are:
- use Exclusions -> None
- define the function so it evaluates only numerically, for example f[x_?NumericQ] := Piecewise[...]

That usually makes Plot use numeric values and avoids spurious vertical segments or gaps.

q: Dealing with square roots
ans:
If you want to deal with square roots in a quadratic-related expression, the closest supported approach is to solve for the variable first, then expand the resulting root as a series and extract coefficients.

For example:
`sol = Z /. Solve[F[Z, a[x], b[x], c[x]] == 0, Z];`
`sol2 = Series[sol, {x, x0, n}];`
`coeff = Table[Coefficient[sol2, x, i], {i, 1, n}];`

If the square root appears in multiple branches, this gives coefficients for each branch. If the expression is too complicated, take the series first, then use `Normal[sol2]` for the truncated polynomial.

q: Assigning the answer of Solve to a variable
ans:
Yes. Store the output of `Solve` in a variable, then use replacement rules to pull values out and reuse them in later calculations.

For example:

`sol = Solve[...]`

Then extract a value like this:

`y[1] /. sol[[1]]`

This uses the first rule set returned by `Solve` and substitutes it into `y[1]`. If `Solve` returns multiple solutions, select the one you want from `sol` and apply `/.` to get the corresponding variable values for subsequent calculations.

q: Using implicit differentiation to find a line that is tangent to a curve at a point
ref:
Certainly, there is a better way:

y[x_] := 2 x Sin[x]; a = Pi/2;
Collect[Normal[Series[y[x], {x, a, 1}]], x, Simplify]

Recall that the formula for a Taylor polynomial looks a bit like this:

$$f(x)=\color{red}{f(a)+f^\prime (a)(x-a)}+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(a)}{2}(x-a)^2+\cdots$$

and reconciling this with the geometric interpretation of the Taylor polynomial as the best one-point osculatory (agrees at function and derivative values) approximation of a function shows why the approach works. I believe this should be a standard way to look at Taylor polynomials in the textbooks, if it already isn't.

Here is an equivalent approach:

Collect[InterpolatingPolynomial[{{{a}, y[a], y'[a]}}, x], x, Simplify]

This is based on the fact that the tangent line is the unique Hermite interpolating polynomial of degree $1$.

Certainly, one could do the plodding, "traditional" (whatever that means) approach:

y[x_] := 2 x Sin[x]; a = Pi/2;
Collect[y[a] + y'[a] (x - a), x, Simplify]

In any event, Solve[] is definitely unnecessary here.
ans:
If the curve is given as y = f(x), first find the slope by differentiating to get f'(x), then evaluate it at the point x = a. The tangent line is

y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)

If the curve is given parametrically, use the derivative vector of the parametrization at the given parameter value as the tangent direction, together with the point on the curve.

If you want to use implicit differentiation, it serves the same purpose: find dy/dx from the implicit equation, evaluate it at the point, then plug that slope into the tangent line formula above.

q: Representation of negative exponents
ref:
Since this has been bumped by Community, I'll post this in the hopes that either @swish will also post it and take credit, or at least @Kagaratsch will accept this so it won't be left unanswered:

  Try this /. Exp[n_?Negative x_] :> 0 – swish Apr 24 at 23:00
ans:
If you want a rule to apply to a negative exponent, match the structure of the exponent, not a literal text form.

For example, a pattern like

`expr /. Exp[n_?Negative x_] :> 0`

is the supported approach shown here for matching an exponential with a negative exponent form.

A rule like `Exp[-x_] -> 0` is too literal and may not match the expression structure you expect. If you share the exact expression form, I can help adapt the pattern.

q: Why evaluation doesn't fail if arguments are invalid?
ref:
Without going into too much detail, this is a result of the way pattern matching is carried out. When you write the rule f[y_]:={x,y} for instance, it tells the compiler that it should match anything and call it y, then replace any instance of y on the right side with the match. But x doesn't evaluate until after this has already happend. A good way to see what goes on is to use Trace

x = 5 y;
f[y_] := {x, y}
f[3] // Trace

(*=>  {f[3],{x,3},{x,5 y},{5 y,3}} *)

The way to get around this is to get x to evaluate before you define the rule, which you can do for instance by passing it through an anonomous function: 

(f[y_] := {#, y})&@x
f[3] // Trace
(*=>  {f[3],{5 3,3},{5 3,15},{15,3}} *)

If you want to see why this works out you can see that at the time the rule definition is evaluated x has been fully replace by using Trace on the code defining the function

 (f[y_] := {#, y}) &@x // Trace

(*=> {{x,5 y},((f[y_]:={#1,y})&)[5 y],f[y_]:={5 y,y},Null} *)
ans:
The evidence only shows that argument evaluation happens before pattern matching, and that a matched argument is not re-evaluated afterward. It does not explain why evaluation would continue when arguments are invalid.

The closest supported guidance is that evaluation timing matters: if you need a value to be computed before a definition uses it, force that evaluation explicitly, for example with an anonymous function like `(function1[y_] := {#, y}) &@x`.

So this evidence covers evaluation order, not error handling for invalid arguments.

q: Assigning the answer of Solve to a variable
ref:
How do you like this:

a = 3 x + 5 == 2;
Subtract[#, 2] & /@ a

(* 3 + 3 x == 0 *)

Edit:
(according to rcollyer's advice)

Subtract[#, 2] & /@(3 x + 5 == 2)

Edit:
(according to J.M's advice)

(#-2)&/@(3 x + 5 == 2)
ans:
Store the output of Solve in a variable:

sol = Solve[3 x + 5 == 2, x]

If you want the result wrapped in a list, use braces:

{Solve[3 x + 5 == 2, x]}

q: Filter sublists that contain a certain value
ref:
Select[GatherBy[{{1, a}, {10, a}, {5, b}, {4, c}}, Last], Length[#] > 1 &]

seems to do what you want. Alternatives to this construction include:

DeleteCases[GatherBy[{{1, a}, {10, a}, {5, b}, {4, c}}, Last], {_List}]

and

ans:

`Select[GatherBy[data, Last], Length[#] > 1 &]`

This works by grouping sublists with the same value and selecting groups with length greater than 1. If your goal is slightly different, the same pattern applies: group by the target value, then filter the groups you want.

q: Unexpected behavior of rule matching a pattern
ref:
Without going into too much detail, this is a result of the way pattern matching is carried out. When you write the rule f[y_]:={x,y} for instance, it tells the compiler that it should match anything and call it y, then replace any instance of y on the right side with the match. But x doesn't evaluate until after this has already happend. A good way to see what goes on is to use Trace

x = 5 y;
f[y_] := {x, y}
f[3] // Trace

(*=>  {f[3],{x,3},{x,5 y},{5 y,3}} *)

The way to get around this is to get x to evaluate before you define the rule, which you can do for instance by passing it through an anonomous function: 

(f[y_] := {#, y})&@x
f[3] // Trace
(*=>  {f[3],{5 3,3},{5 3,15},{15,3}} *)

If you want to see why this works out you can see that at the time the rule definition is evaluated x has been fully replace by using Trace on the code defining the function

 (f[y_] := {#, y}) &@x // Trace

(*=> {{x,5 y},((f[y_]:={#1,y})&)[5 y],f[y_]:={5 y,y},Null} *)

Your rule is probably keeping `x` unevaluated when the pattern rule is stored, so the right-hand side ends up containing a symbolic `x` and only gets matched later. That can leave the result unevaluated.

When you make a copy, `x` is forced to evaluate first, so the value is fixed into the definition before the rule is stored.

The closest supported fix is to evaluate `x` at definition time, for example by wrapping it in an anonymous function so the stored rule contains the evaluated expression instead of `x`.

q: Assigning the answer of Solve to a variable
ans:
Yes. Capture the output of `Solve` in a variable, then extract the values you need with replacement rules.

For example:

`sol = Solve[...];`

Then use:

`y[1] /. sol[[1]]`

This takes the first rule set returned by `Solve` and substitutes it into `y[1]`. If there are multiple solutions, select the appropriate solution from `sol` and apply `/.` to get the corresponding variable values.

q: What is the precision of this number?
ref:
For the sake of alternatives, here's another way.  You can specify a precision with a backtick.  This is called an "arbitrary-precision" number.  Such numbers are treated differently than machine precision numbers.

Examples of 3 and 5 digits of precision:    

16.`3

16.0

16.`5

16.000

Machine precision depends on the machine, but it's often nearly 16 digits.

$MachinePrecision

15.9546

The results of your calculation at different precisions are given below.  Note they are more accurate than machine precision, even though the specified precisions are technically less.  That's because Mathematica can use up to $MaxExtraPrecision extra digits of precision in its internal calculations.

1/Sqrt[1 - (150^2 10^(-4))/(9 10^16.`3)] - 1
1/Sqrt[1 - (150^2 10^(-4))/(9 10^16.`4)] - 1
1/Sqrt[1 - (150^2 10^(-4))/(9 10^16.`5)] - 1
1/Sqrt[1 - (150^2 10^(-4))/(9 10^16.`15)] - 1

1.3*10^-17    
1.25*10^-17  
1.250*10^-17  
1.2500000000000*10^-17

Which way is better, this one or using N and exact numbers as in the answers of @chuy and @m_goldberg?  Well it depends. Normally N[exact] is sufficient, although in this case, it fails -- it gives 0.  Arbitrary-precision calculations take longer, but Mathematica does try to keep track of the precision as it goes along.  On the other hand, N[exact, prec] (@m_goldberg's answer) tracks the precision and, more importantly, it gives an answer with the target precision, if the internal precision limit $MaxExtraPrecision is not exceeded.

Update: Altern
ans:
The evidence only says to use double floating-point precision / machine-precision numbers, but it does not give the precision of a specific number.

Closest guidance: if the number is stored as a machine-precision float, it is about double precision, typically around 16 decimal digits of precision. If you need an exact precision for a particular value, I’d need the number itself.

q: How to extract data from a list?
ref:
How about mapping Position like so

Position[listb, #] & /@ lista
(*{{{3}}, {{4}}, {{5}}, {{6}}, {{7}}, {{8}}, {{9}}, {{1}}, {{2}}}*)

which gives the position of each sublist of lista in listb?

To get only the first instance, use

Position[listb, #, 1, 1] & /@ lista

(the last argument of Position specifies how many positions found to return; the penultimate argument specifies the level at which to search).
ans:
If you want to extract a specific element from each sublist, map `Part` over the list.

For the second element of each sublist:

`#[[2]] & /@ lista`

or

`Part[#, 2] & /@ lista`

This returns the item at position 2 from every sublist. If your lists have different lengths, you may need extra handling for sublists that don’t contain that position.

q: Reuse local variable in declaration within With
ref:
The third argument of ToExpression with the Trott–Strzebonski can be used to do this:

HoldComplete[g["x"]] /. s_String :> 
    With[{x = ToExpression[s, InputForm, Defer]}, x /; True]
(* HoldComplete[g[x]] *)
ans:
The supported pattern is to assign the local variable from `ToExpression[..., InputForm, Defer]` inside `With`, so the value stays unevaluated:

`HoldComplete[g["x"]] /. s_String :> With[{x = ToExpression[s, InputForm, Defer]}, x /; True]`

That produces `HoldComplete[g[x]]`.

If your input is `InputForm@HoldComplete[g["x"]]`, this same approach can leave an extra `Defer`, giving `HoldComplete[g[Defer[x]]]`, so you may need to strip `Defer` afterward in that case.

q: sliding a tangent line along a curve
Using the result of Solve in subsequent calculations
ref:
Undocumented Method->"Legacy" option forces Solve in version 8 to use algorithm from versions <=7. 

exprs = Together[{(b + d + f)/x - (a + b)/(1 + x) - 
     2*(c + d + e)/(1 + 2*x + y) - (f + g)/(x + y), (e + g)/
      y - (c + d + e)/(1 + 2*x + y) - (f + g)/(x + y)}];
Timing[solns1 = Solve[exprs == 0, {x, y}, Method -> "Legacy"];]

  {39.515, Null}

q: Plotting a curve in 3D
ref:
You question is not completely clear. What you can do is the following: You make a 2d contour plot of your second equation and transform this into a 3d graphics by appending a 0 (z=0) to all Line points appearing in the 2d graphics and turning the lines into Tube's:

Show[
 ContourPlot3D[{x^2 + y^2 == z, 2 y == z, 
   x^2 + (y \[Minus] 1/2)^2 == 1}, {x, -2, 2}, {y, -0.5, 1}, {z, 0, 
   2}, ContourStyle -> Opacity[.3]],
 Graphics3D[{Red, 
   Cases[Normal[
     ContourPlot[x^2 + (y - 1/2)^2 == 1, {x, -2, 2}, {y, -1/2, 1}]], 
    Line[pts_] :> Tube[Append[#, 0] & /@ pts], Infinity]}],
 PlotRange -> All
 ]
ans:
The supported approach is to draw the 2D curve and then lift it into 3D by giving every point a zero z-coordinate, then combine it with other 3D graphics using Show.

The example method uses ContourPlot, Normal, Cases[..., Line[pts_] :> ...], and Append[#, 0] & /@ pts.

This only covers plotting a 2D shape in 3D. It does not provide a direct method for finding the area, an algebraic equation for the curve, or a jaggedness measure for an arbitrary shape.

 {t, -80, 80},

Based upon Karsten's comment and Michael's review a complete solution set could look like this:

  Point[{{-1, 0}, {1, 0}}]

  Point[{{0, -1}, {0, 1}}]

  ParametricPlot[{f2[t], g2[t]},
   {t, -80, 80},
   PlotRange -> {{-4, 4}, {-2, 4}},
   Exclusions -> t == 0,
   Epilog -> {PointSize[0.02], {Blue, pf}, {Red, pg}},
   PlotStyle -> Green,

leg =
  SwatchLegend[{Green, Blue, Red}, {"{f2[t], g2[t]} != 0", "f2[t] == 0", "g2[t] == 0"}];

Legended[par, leg]
ans:
To remove the unwanted flat parts, exclude the parameter values or regions that create them.

If the flats come from a specific condition, use Exclusions in the plot, for example:

Plot3D[expr, {x, xmin, xmax}, {y, ymin, ymax},
 Exclusions -> condition]

If you only want to hide the unwanted part, you can also use ExclusionsStyle.

If you need the missing piece shown separately, the supported approach is to split the surface into valid and invalid parts and add back any special points or edges separately.

q: Evaluating a function using arguments from a sliding window over a list
ans:
Yes. You can evaluate a function with arguments taken from a list using Apply (`@@`), and you can build the function with `Evaluate` if the parameters come from a list of symbols.

For a sliding window, the same idea applies: take each window from the list, then apply the function to that window with `@@`.

For example, if your window size is 2:

`windows = Partition[list, 2, 1];`
`results = (f @@ #) & /@ windows;`

If the arguments are stored as symbols, keep them in held form like `Hold[a, b]` and substitute them into `Function` before applying it.

q: How do I remove the flat parts that are not part of the function in Plot3D?
ref:
When Mathematica automatically determines the plot range, it sometimes decides to clip off the very high or very low parts of the graph.  It does this, I suppose, when including the extreme parts of the range results in a plot that is flattened too much.  If you don't want this, Mathematica also supplies easy options to override the automatic behavior.

Try PlotRange -> All:

Plot3D[0.25*(1/(1 - 0.9*(1 - bn))) ((1 - bn)/(1 - 0.5*bn))^2,
 {bn, 0, 1}, {bu, 0, 1}, RegionFunction -> Function[{bn, bu}, bn > bu], 
 PlotRange -> All]

Only a small part of the graph above sticks up high.  With the setting PlotRange -> Automatic, Mathematica decides to chop part of it off.  Without the restriction by RegionFunction, as in the OP's second plot, the high part runs along the whole bu axis.  In that case, Mathematica doesn't cut it off.   If it were steeper it would cut it off:

Plot3D[0.25*(1/(1 - 0.95*(1 - bn))) ((1 - bn)/(1 - 0.5*bn))^2,
 {bn, 0,1}, {bu, 0, 1}]
ans:
The flat parts are likely from automatic plot-range clipping, not from Plot3D itself. Try setting PlotRange -> All so the full surface is shown instead of the steep region being flattened or cut off.

Example:

Plot3D[expr, {x, xmin, xmax}, {y, ymin, ymax}, PlotRange -> All]

If you’re also using RegionFunction, keep it and still add PlotRange -> All.

q: Scoping problem with Manipulate
ref:
Any issues with this?

Manipulate[
 Plot[ReleaseHold[eqn /. Symbol[$Context <> "r"] :> r], {x, -5, 5}] //
   Dynamic, 
 Grid[{{"r=", 
    Control[{{r, -1, ""}, -2, 2, .1, 
      Appearance -> "Labeled"}]}, {"eqn", 
    InputField[Dynamic[eqn], Hold@Expression], 
    Dynamic[HoldForm @@ eqn]}}], {{r, -2}, None}, {{eqn, Null}, None},
 Initialization :> 
  ToExpression["r", InputForm, 
   Function[r, eqn = Hold[r + x], HoldFirst]]]

When you evaluate, for example

DynamicModule[{x = 0},
 Button["Increment", ++x]]

it does something similar to a Module except that the result is again wrapped in DynamicModule. So in this case it retuns (almost) the exact same expression, but in the process, the kernel creates a variable (like Module would) and stores it.
Even though the front end "owns" x, the kernel has it's copy. And this copy has some local ugly unique name that guarantees no conflicts.
In many dynamic updates, Mathematica simply assumes that the value the kernel has is correct, so it doesn't need to sync it and saves time. So, it just sends to the kernel the dynamic code with xs replaced by the corresponding FE`x$29whatever.
Now, if your code has a line such as Symbol["x"], that won't be recognized as the symbol x until the kernel already has the code and is evaluating it. So, it simply becomes the variable x in the current context. In the version in this answer, that "r" in the current context is replaced by whatever local variable Mathematica automatically replaces r with.
ans:
Inside Manipulate, the control variable is locally scoped, so the symbol name inside the body may not refer to the global variable you defined outside. That’s the scoping issue, not the computation itself.

The supported workaround is to avoid depending on the raw name inside a string expression. Instead, either replace the local control symbol before plotting, or convert the string to a held expression during initialization with Hold/ReleaseHold, or use an InputField with Dynamic that holds the expression.

If you want, I can help rewrite your specific Manipulate code using one of those approaches.

q: What causes strange line artifacts to appear in plots with certain PlotRanges?
ref:
As you already know from the comments, increasing MaxRecursion or PlotPoints helps, where I would prefer the first one.

In the case of your function, you can gain some speed by compiling the expression. Then, you can set MaxRecursion to a higher value and the plot is still reasonable fast. The code below runs in about 3 seconds here

m = 60;
With[{cf = (Compile[{{x, _Real, 0}, {y, _Real, 0}},
        #, RuntimeOptions -> "Speed", CompilationTarget -> "C"] & /@

           Flatten[{Re[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]], 
        Im[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]]}])},
  (#1[args__?NumericQ] := #2[args]) & @@@ Transpose[{{f1, f2}, cf}]
  ];

ContourPlot[{f1[x, y], f2[x, y]}, {x, -5, 6}, {y, -10, 10}, 
 AspectRatio -> Automatic, MaxRecursion -> 3]
ans:
Strange line artifacts or breaks are usually caused by insufficient sampling. The first thing to try is increasing MaxRecursion; PlotPoints can also help, but MaxRecursion is the better first choice.

If the plot is slow, compiling the expressions can help keep higher recursion levels fast. Using a plot with higher MaxRecursion should reduce the broken-looking sections.

q: Simple Macro or Meta Programming for Data Analysis
ans:
For elementwise selection, the fastest reported approach was a vectorized `UnitStep` expression rather than looping or using `If` inside `Table`.

You can use:
`v3 = UnitStep[v1] (v1 - v2) + v2`

or:
`v3 = UnitStep[v1] v1 + (1 - UnitStep[v1]) v2`

This was reported faster than `Boole` and explicit loops, with `Clip` close behind. If you need sparse updates, a `SparseArray`-based index approach was also noted as competitive.

ans:

`Cases[list, {x_, y_} :> y]`

If you need to extract second values only from pairs whose first element matches a condition, use:

`Cases[list, {x_, y_} /; rule[x] :> y]`

If your sublists have a different shape, the pattern needs to be adjusted.

q: Combining the second elements of a set of ordered pairs based on their first element
ref:
You can achieve the same end with DeleteCases or Cases.

f signals a coordinate that is out of bounds.

g signals that a coordinate is in bounds.

f[n_] := n < 1 \[Or] n > 9
g[n_] := 1 <= n <= 9

Four ways to filter out the outlying points: 

v[k] generates  10^k values between {0, 0} and {10, 10})

v[k_] := Table[{r, r}, {10^k}];

Delete the points that have an out-of-bounds coordinate.

DeleteCases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; f[x] \[Or] f[y]]

Delete the points that are not in-bounds.

DeleteCases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; \[Not] (g[x] \[And] g[y])]

Keep points that are not out-of-bounds.

Cases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; \[Not] (f[x] \[Or] f[y])]

Keep points that are in-bounds.

Cases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; (g[x] \[And] g[y])]

Timings

    r = Table[{AbsoluteTiming[DeleteCases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; f[x] \[Or] f[y]];],
          AbsoluteTiming[DeleteCases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; \[Not] (g[x] \[And]g[y])];], 
          AbsoluteTiming[Cases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; \[Not] (f[x] \[Or] f[y])];],
          AbsoluteTiming[Cases[v[k], {x_, y_} /; (g[x] \[And] g[y])];]}, {k,  3, 7}]
    Grid@Prepend[ r[[All, All, 1]], {"Delete f", "Delete not-g", "Cases not-f", "Cases g"}]

The results with DeleteCases and Cases (from 10^3  to 10^7 points)
show that DeleteCases with function  g gives the fastest analysis.
ans:
If you want the second elements from pairs that share the same first element, you can use pattern-based selection on the list of ordered pairs and then extract the second part.

For example, to keep pairs with a given first element `x0` and get their second elements:

`Cases[list, {x0, y_} :> y]`

If you want all second elements grouped by first element, you’d need to collect/group the pairs first, then combine or extract the second components from each group. The provided pattern-based forms support selecting pairs, but they don’t by themselves do the grouping/combining step.

q: Is there a way to add arrows along a parametric curve inside a manipulate function?
ans:
Yes. A workable approach is to place a rotated arrow on the curve and animate it with the parameter in Manipulate.

For example, for a circle:

Manipulate[
 Graphics[{Circle[], Rotate[Arrow[{{1, 0}, {1, 1}}], φ, {0, 0}]}],
 {φ, 0, 2 Pi}
]

For a general parametric curve, use ArcTan[x, y] to get the tangent direction instead of calculating a slope manually, since it handles vertical tangents more safely. Then position the arrow at the curve point and rotate it by that angle.

q: How can I replace very small scientific form of numbers in output with 0.0?

StandardForm@NumberForm[1.2, {20, 4}, ExponentFunction -> (Null &)]
(* 1.2000 *)
StandardForm@NumberForm[1., {20, 4}, ExponentFunction -> (Null &)]
(* 1.0000 *)
StandardForm@NumberForm[0.2, {20, 4}, ExponentFunction -> (Null &)]

ans:

`StandardForm@NumberForm[x, {20, 4}, ExponentFunction -> (Null &)]`

This forces a fixed decimal display, so very small numbers print as ordinary decimals instead of scientific form. If the value is exactly zero, it can also display as `0.0000` instead of `0.`. The underlying value is unchanged; only the displayed form changes. If you want a specific `0.0` style, adjust the second argument to control the number of decimal places.

q: Storing solution to x and y
ref:
Undocumented Method->"Legacy" option forces Solve in version 8 to use algorithm from versions <=7. 

exprs = Together[{(b + d + f)/x - (a + b)/(1 + x) - 
     2*(c + d + e)/(1 + 2*x + y) - (f + g)/(x + y), (e + g)/
      y - (c + d + e)/(1 + 2*x + y) - (f + g)/(x + y)}];
Timing[solns1 = Solve[exprs == 0, {x, y}, Method -> "Legacy"];]

  {39.515, Null}

Solve[exprs == 0, {x, y}] never returns in version 8. Additional examples see here.

Some information on the change in the algorithm between versions 7 and 8 is published by Bruce Miller (Wolfram Technical Support Group):

  Boilerplate I had:

  
  The difference between 7.0 and 8.0 output is that 7.0 Solve was
  treating equations that involved only variables as assumptions. This
  functionality was not precisely defined or consistently implemented
  and has been removed in 8.0.  Instead there is a new option
  MaxExtraConditions which provides a well-defined and extended version
  of the functionality.
ans:

For example:

Then use sol in later calculations, or place it in a list assignment if needed. If you need a specific list form, that depends on the exact structure Solve returns.

q: How can I solve precision problem
ref:
Control the Precision and Accuracy of Numerical Results

This is an excellent question.

Of course everyone could claim highest accuracy for their product.

To deal with this situation there exist benchmarks to test for accuracy.

One such benchmark is from NIST. This specific benchmark deals with the accuracy of statistical software for instance.

The NIST StRD benchmark provides reference datasets with certified computational results that enable the objective evaluation of statistical software.

In an old issue of The Mathematica Journal, Marc Nerlove writes elaborately about performing the linear and nonlinear regressions using the NIST StRD benchmark (and  Kernel developer Darren Glosemeyer from WRI discussing results using Mathematica version 5.1).

Numerically unstable functions:

But this is only one part of story. OK. There exist benchmark for statistical software etc., but what happens if we take some functions that are numerically unstable? 

Stan Wagon has several examples of inaccuracies and how to deal with them in his book Mathematica in Action, which I can only warmly suggest. I have it now for (the latest edition) several years and everytime there is something new to discover with Mr. Wagon.

Let's take, for instance a numerical unstable Maclaurin polynomial of $\sin x$:

poly = Normal[Series[Sin[x], {x, 0, 200}]];
Plot[poly, {x, 0, 100}, PlotRange -> {-2, 2}, 
    PlotStyle -> {Thickness[0.0010], Black}]

The result this we can see that the result breaks down
ans:
If you need reliable decimal accuracy, the supported approach is to request higher precision and see whether the result stays stable. In Mathematica, use N[expr, n] to ask for n digits and trust only the digits Mathematica can track through the computation.

Mathematica tracks precision through many arbitrary-precision calculations and suppresses digits that may be affected by uncertain input. So if increasing the requested precision does not change the reported digits, those digits are more likely to be correct.

If you want, I can help you check a specific expression for precision issues.

q: Why does the Front End group backslashes into pairs?
ref:
Your sample output seems inconsistent - either you list all elements, including those that are only present in just one pair, or you should not have things like {{9,7}}. Assuming the first scenario, here is a possibility:

DeleteDuplicates[Reap[Sow[#, #] & /@ pairs][[2]]]

(*
{        
    {{1,2}},
    {{1,2},{2,5},{2,6}},
    {{3,4}},
    {{3,4},{5,4}},
    {{2,5},{5,4}},
    {{2,6}},
    {{9,7}}
}
*)

You can filter out the cases with just one pair by applying Select[#,Length[#]>1&]& to the above result.
ans:
Backslashes are grouped into pairs because the Front End is treating them as elements to be counted/grouped, and the same grouping idea applies: identical items are collected together. In this case, a pair of backslashes is often the displayed result of grouping repeated backslashes, since one backslash is an escape character and may be shown doubled in text form.

The closest guidance supported here is that if you want to count or group by a shared first element, use grouping by that key, like `CountsBy[pairs, First]` or `Reap/Sow` with `Length` on each group.

q: Dealing with square roots
ref:
Here's a way to do it numerically. It uses the adaptive sampling Plot uses to determine the approximate positions of the roots.

Here's the expression:

expr = x^2*Log[2, (3 + x)/10] - 
   x^2*Log[1/2, 2 + 3*x] - (x^2 - 4 + 
     2*Log[Sqrt[2], (3*x^2 + 11*x + 6)/10]);

We'll solve for expr==0. We look for roots between 

xlow = 0; xhigh = 3;

To do that, ask Plot to plot the expression, then extract the list of data points:

(points = 
   Cases[Normal[Plot[expr, {x, xlow, xhigh}]], Line[l_] :> l, 
     Infinity] // First) // Shallow

These are the points Plot uses. You can ListPlot them to see the adaptive sampling at play.

Now, we need to locate which two points bracket a root, which means that their y-coordinates have opposite signs; so check for this:

signChanges = Position[
   Times @@ ## & /@ Partition[points[[All, 2]], 2, 1],
   x_ /; x < 0
   ] // Flatten

{23, 232}

and finally use FindRoot giving it a range to search in:

FindRoot[expr == 0, {x, points[[#, 1]], points[[# + 1, 1]]}] & /@ signChanges
{{x -> 1.}, {x -> 2.}}

EDIT: changed the way the points are obtained after discussion with Artes and JM
ans:
To deal with square roots in an equation, you can square both sides to remove them. Raise each side to the second power, but be careful: this can create extra solutions, so always check your answers in the original equation.

For example, if √x = 3, squaring both sides gives x = 9.

If you share the exact equation, I can show the steps.

q: Mathematica issue with Plot, D and SetDelayed
ref:
As you already know from the comments, increasing MaxRecursion or PlotPoints helps, where I would prefer the first one.

In the case of your function, you can gain some speed by compiling the expression. Then, you can set MaxRecursion to a higher value and the plot is still reasonable fast. The code below runs in about 3 seconds here

m = 60;
With[{cf = (Compile[{{x, _Real, 0}, {y, _Real, 0}},
        #, RuntimeOptions -> "Speed", CompilationTarget -> "C"] & /@

           Flatten[{Re[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]], 
        Im[Table[BernoulliB[n, (x + I y)], {n, m, m}]]}])},
  (#1[args__?NumericQ] := #2[args]) & @@@ Transpose[{{f1, f2}, cf}]
  ];

ContourPlot[{f1[x, y], f2[x, y]}, {x, -5, 6}, {y, -10, 10}, 
 AspectRatio -> Automatic, MaxRecursion -> 3]
ans:
A break in a Plot/Plot3D result is usually caused by insufficient sampling. The first thing to try is increasing MaxRecursion; PlotPoints can also help, but MaxRecursion is the better first choice.

If the expression is slow to evaluate, compiling the parts you need can help keep higher recursion levels fast. For example, compile the real and imaginary parts into functions and then plot those.

If you want, I can also help you adapt this to your specific Plot, D, and SetDelayed setup, but the main fix supported here is to increase MaxRecursion and, if needed, PlotPoints.

q: Plotting complex numbers
ans:
To plot a complex number or complex-valued function in the complex plane, use its real part as the x-coordinate and its imaginary part as the y-coordinate. For a function f(x), plot the pair (\Re f(x), \Im f(x)).

If you want to visualize the parameter as well, you can use a 3D parametric plot with the real part, imaginary part, and the parameter as axes, for example:

ParametricPlot3D[{-Re[f[x]], Im[f[x]], x}, {x, 0, 5 Pi}]

This gives a 3D curve rather than a 2D complex-plane plot.

q: How to create functions of arbitrary number of variables?
ans:
For a fixed number of variables, define the function with patterns for each argument, for example:

`functionName[arg1_, arg2_, arg3_] := Module[{local1, local2}, ...; result]`

If you need code that changes often or has repeated parts, wrap the repeated parts into a function and use local variables rather than repeatedly clearing globals. You can also define local helper functions inside the main function.

This does not give the exact syntax for truly variable-length argument lists, only the general approach to function definitions and local scoping.

q: Replacing values above a threshold with 1
ref:
Here's an example of a way to do this.

list = RandomInteger[5, 20]

(* {5, 1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 0, 4, 0, 3, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1, 5, 2, 5, 4, 3} *)

rules = {1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, 3 -> 4, 9 -> 8};

ReplacePart[list, Cases[Thread[Position[list, #, 1, 1] & /@ rules[[All, 1]] -> 
            rules[[All, 2]]], ({{a_}} -> b_) :> a -> b]]

(* {5, 2, 4, 3, 2, 2, 0, 4, 0, 3, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1, 5, 2, 5, 4, 3} *)

This works by finding the position of the first occurrence (if it exists) for each left-hand side of the rules, and re-writing the rules to use that position in place of the value.

Pretty snappy, if you need it faster that can be done at the cost of more convoluted code.

Update: Based on Mr.Wizard's comments, perhaps this is more in line with desired results:

repper[list_, rules_, depth_: 1] := 
 Module[{rg = GatherBy[rules, First], m1, rp},
  m1 = Map[Position[list, #[[1]], depth, #[[2]]] &, Tally[rules[[All, 1]]]];
  rp = Flatten@MapIndexed[# -> rg[[Sequence @@ #2]][[2]] &, m1, {2}];
  ReplacePart[list, rp]]

list = {1.25, 1, 2, 3, 5.5, 20, 30};

rules = {_Integer -> 4, _Integer -> 5, _Integer -> 6, _Real -> 2.5, _Integer -> 66,
         3 -> 999};

repper[list, rules]

(* {2.5, 4, 5, 6, 5.5, 66, 30} *)

repper[foo[1, {2, 3, 0, 1/3}], 
       {_Integer -> 4, _Integer -> 5, _Integer -> 6, foo -> bar, _Rational -> 2.5},
       Infinity]

(* bar[4, {5, 6, 0, 2.5}] *)
ans:
Use position-based replacement: find the elements above the threshold with Position, then replace those positions with 1 using ReplacePart.

For example, the supported pattern is:
- locate matching elements with Position,
- then apply ReplacePart to set those positions to 1.

If you want, I can help turn that into the exact Wolfram Language expression for your threshold and data structure.

q: Why evaluation doesn't fail if arguments are invalid?
ref:
IfBuilt-in Mathematica symbol

  If[condition,t,f,u]
  gives u if condition evaluates to neither True nor False. 

x = 1;
For[i = 1, i <= 3, i++,
 If[x + i > notDefined, x = 100, , Throw["myError"]];
 Print[StringJoin["i = ", ToString[i], ", x = ", ToString[x]]];]

  Throw::nocatch: Uncaught Throw[myError] returned to top level. >>
ans:
Evaluation doesn’t fail because `If` only proceeds when its condition becomes `True` or `False`. If the condition stays unevaluated, `If` does not evaluate the then/else branch, and by default it just does nothing.

So invalid-looking arguments won’t necessarily trigger a failure if they prevent the condition from resolving. The supported way to catch that is to handle the unevaluated case explicitly, for example with the 4th argument of `If`, such as `Throw["myError"]`.

Refine[If[t - u < 0, Print[Yes], Print[No]], $Assumptions]

Yes

The last line is also the way it would look if you were to wrap your If statement in Assuming. However, since $Assumptions is also used by default, you can simply do this:

Assuming[t < u, Refine[If[t - u < 0, Print[Yes], Print[No]]]]

Yes
ans:
If the condition is symbolic, `If` may not evaluate by itself. Wrap the expression in `Refine` so the condition can be resolved under assumptions.

For example:

`Assuming[t < u, Refine[If[t - u < 0, Print[Yes], Print[No]]]]`

or:

`Refine[If[t - u < 0, Print[Yes], Print[No]], t < u]`

If you want it applied globally, set:

`$Assumptions = t < u;`

then use `Refine[...]`.

The provided guidance only says you can fill regions associated with curves using `Filling` with `Show` or `Piecewise`, but it does not give a direct point-in-polygon method.

Closest practical approach: if you have a specific closed curve, adapt the filling/region idea to that curve and test whether the point lies in the enclosed region. If you share the curve form, I can help set up the exact test.

q: How to define the tangent gradient operator?
ref:
I guess a more complex expression as exponent should be converted into a box structure as well. Why don't you just put another ToBoxes to convert the exponent?

Operator /: MakeBoxes[Operator[pow_, sym_], fmt_] := 
 With[{sbox = If[StringQ[sym], sym, ToBoxes[sym]]}, 
  With[{abox = SuperscriptBox[#, ToBoxes[pow]] &@sbox}, 
   InterpretationBox[abox, Operator[pow, sym]]]]

Since Kuba's comment says it doesn't work without a HoldForm I'll put a screenshot. Feel free to insert a hold if it doesn't work for you either

  

If you want to make it more robust for situations where variables have values you could make a slight change:

Attributes[Operator] = {HoldFirst};
Operator /: MakeBoxes[Operator[pow_, sym_], fmt_] := 
 With[{sbox = If[StringQ[sym], sym, ToBoxes[sym]]}, 
  With[{abox = SuperscriptBox[#, ToBoxes[HoldForm[pow]]] &@sbox}, 
   InterpretationBox[abox, Operator[pow, sym]]]]

Now, even something like Operator[1 + 1, x] works, although I don't know whether this is wanted.
ans:
The supported pattern is to define it by giving the operator a custom box form with `MakeBoxes`, then wrap the displayed form in `InterpretationBox` so it still behaves as your operator symbol.

So for a tangent gradient operator, the closest guidance is the same: build its visual representation from boxes using `ToBoxes` for any symbolic parts, and return an `InterpretationBox[...]` around the final layout. 

The evidence does not show the exact tangent-gradient syntax, only the general method for defining an operator’s display and evaluation behavior.

q: Do I have to code each case of this Grid full of plots separately?
ref:
Here's one way that straigthforwardly makes a table of plots:

Table[Plot[{Sum[c[[n]]*LegendreP[n, x], {n, 1, M}], f[x]}, {x, -1, 1},
     PlotStyle -> {{Red}, {Thick, Blue}}, GridLines -> Automatic], {M, {10, 20, 50}}]
ans: No. The supported guidance here says to use Table to generate one plot for each case, so you can make multiple plots with different parameter values without coding each one separately. It does not describe a special way to build a single “Grid full of plots” beyond that, but it does support generating each plot through Table rather than writing each case by hand.

q: What is wrong with ContourPlot
ref:
I extend my comment to decrease the number of unanswered questions.

Just add PlotRange -> All

ContourPlot[Exp[-x^2 - y^2], {x, -3, 3}, {y, -3, 3}]

ContourPlot[Exp[-x^2 - y^2], {x, -3, 3}, {y, -3, 3}, PlotRange -> All]

q: Picking certain pairs according to a condition
ans:
If the condition is based on the first element, the supported approach is to group the pairs by that first element and then collect the corresponding second elements.

For example, `{{a, x}, {b, y}, {a, z}}` becomes `{{a, {x, z}}, {b, {y}}}` or an equivalent grouped form.

If you mean selecting only certain pairs rather than merging them, the evidence only supports grouping by a key and combining matches; it doesn’t provide a direct rule for arbitrary pair-picking conditions.

q: What is the precision of this number?
ref:
Initially I forgot to specifically address Manipulate.  In addition to this post see also:

Manipulating an arbitrary-precision ContourPlot

This question may qualify as a duplicate (I'll let the community votes decide) but it has been asked in a different way so I'll answer it anew.

There are two issues that may be confounded here: input syntax and output formatting.

Input syntax

By default a number entered with a decimal point that has less than 18 digits is interpreted as a machine precision number, while one with more is interpreted as arbitrary precision:

12.                             // Precision
2.7182818284590452              // Precision
2718281828459045.2              // Precision
2.71828182845904523536028747135 // Precision

  MachinePrecision

  
  MachinePrecision

  
  MachinePrecision

  
  29.4343

Any number (with or without a decimal point) can be entered with a specific precision by using the ` symbol.  A raw ` means MachinePrecision while e.g. `7 means seven digits of precision:

12`      // Precision
12.3`1   // Precision
3.14`20  // Precision

  MachinePrecision

  
  1.

  
  20.

Arithmetic between arbitrary and machine precision numbers automatically converts to machine precision:

12.3`1 * 17.2 // Precision

  MachinePrecision

See also: Converting to machine precision

Output formatting

Machine precision numbers are by default automatically truncated to six digits in OutputForm, but more digits are still there internally:

2.7182818284590452
ans: The value’s precision isn’t given explicitly. The only supported point is that `N[x, 100]` won’t create extra decimal places for a machine-precision number. To get more displayed digits, the number must have higher internal precision, such as entering it as an arbitrary-precision number like `3.14`20. If you share the actual number, I can help infer whether it’s machine precision or arbitrary precision.

q: How do I obtain the enclosed area of this particular parametric plot?
ref:
Under the interpretation of OP's question as

  How do I apply the transformation $w=f(z)$ to a region (e.g. a disk) in the complex plane?

I'd say ParametricPlot[] (which now incorporates the functionality from the old Graphics`ComplexMap` package) would be what you can use:

With[{f = # + 1/# &, center = 1/3 + 3 I/2, radius = 4/3}, 
 ParametricPlot[
       Through[{Re, Im}[f[center + r Exp[I θ]]]], {r, 0, radius}, {θ, -π, π},
               PlotPoints -> 45, PlotRange -> All]]
ans:
The supported approach is to parameterize the region and plot its image under the complex map. For a disk-like region, use

z = center + r Exp[I θ]

and then plot

Through[{Re, Im}[f[center + r Exp[I θ]]]]

with ParametricPlot.

This tells you how to generate the parametric plot of the transformed region, but it does not directly provide an area formula for that plot. If your region is not disk-like, you need a parameterization of the original region first. Then you can work from that parameterization to represent the boundary or image, but the evidence does not give a direct enclosed-area method.

q: Why evaluation doesn't fail if arguments are invalid?
ref:
It allows partial function application. Observe how function test1 defined this way can be called with the first argument, resulting in the return of another function of the remaining argument. Function test2 does not, and simply returns unevaluated since no match to its pattern occurs.

Clear[test1,test2]

test1[x_][y_]:=x^y
test2[x_,y_]:=x^y

test1[2][3]
(* 8 *)

test2[2,3]
(* 8 *)

test1[2]
(* test1[2] *)

%[3]
(* 8 *)

test2[2]
(* test2[2] *)

%[3]
(* test2[2][3] *)
ans:
Evaluation doesn’t fail here because `Evaluate` only forces an intermediate expression to reduce before more arguments are applied; it does not validate whether the arguments are “valid” in the sense of matching a function definition.

In the `f[x_][y_] := expr` form, `f[2]` already evaluates to something that can accept `y`, so `Evaluate` is usually unnecessary. In the `f[x_, y_] := expr` form, `f[2]` simply doesn’t match, so it cannot be used as a function at all.

So invalid arguments don’t cause `Evaluate` itself to fail; they just determine whether the expression matches a definition.

q: If statements with a Boolean
ref:
No.  Re[x] > 0 means that the real part of x is positive, but it does not mean that the imaginary part is zero.  Re[1+I] > 0 but 1+I is not real.

However, x > 0 is sufficient and (in Mathematica) implies that x is also real.
ans:
`If` only prints the branch whose condition evaluates to the literal Boolean `True`. A condition like `x > 0` under `Assuming` can stay symbolic, so the `Else` branch may be taken or the result may not evaluate as expected.

The supported guidance here is that assumptions do not automatically make such conditions `True`, and `TrueQ` won’t help unless the expression is exactly `True`. If your `If` depends on assumptions, use a test that can reason with them instead of expecting the condition to resolve automatically.
